steps.note: A child for whose benefit a promise was made to her father, on consideration the father supplied, may sue the promisor on it although she neither made the bargain nor furnished the consideration.
A party may not recover for a loss following the other party's breach that he could have avoided by taking available protective action himself.

Whether covenants are independent, dependent or concurrent depends on the evident sense and meaning of the parties and the order of performance the transaction requires, and a party is not liable on its covenant until a condition precedent to it has been fulfilled.

Where a seller's conveyance and a buyer's payment are to be performed at the same time, the promises are dependent, and a party cannot sue on the other's promise without pleading that he performed or offered to perform his own.

Where an express contract makes a lump-sum payment conditional on complete performance, the law will not imply an inconsistent promise to pay proportionately for part performance, even when the performer's blameless death prevented completion.

A clerk discharged without sufficient cause during a quarter who remains willing to serve the rest of it is treated in law as having served the whole quarter and may recover the unpaid salary as a debt for work and labour.

A buyer need not disclose extrinsic information affecting the price where the means of obtaining it are equally accessible to both parties, but neither party may say or do anything tending to impose upon the other.

An offeror who makes an offer by post is treated as making the same offer throughout the letter's journey, and the offeree's acceptance completes the contract without the offeror first having to receive it.
A moral obligation or gratitude for a benefit already conferred, without a prior request or an existing legal obligation of the promisor, is not consideration for a later express promise to pay.

A worker who leaves an entire labor contract without good cause cannot recover on the contract but may recover in quantum meruit the reasonable value of the benefit the employer retained, less the damage caused by the breach and capped by the contract price.
As this 1839 decision held, a buyer's advance notice that he will refuse goods is not itself a breach unless the seller acts on it and rescinds, so damages are measured at the time delivery was due.

An offer that states no time limit lapses after a reasonable time, measured by its terms, purpose, and circumstances; a reward offer answering a particular emergency does not remain open indefinitely merely because it was never formally revoked.
A promise to give a relative a home that is a mere gratuity will not support an action for its breach, even when the promisee incurs loss and inconvenience in moving to receive it.

Equity may enjoin the breach of an express negative promise not to perform elsewhere during an engagement even though it cannot compel affirmative performance of the personal services promised in the same contract.

When one party unequivocally renounces a contract before performance is due, the other may treat it as breached, consider himself released from future performance, and sue immediately for damages, or may instead await the performance date.

Damages for breach of contract are limited to losses that arise naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or that both parties reasonably contemplated, when contracting, as its probable result, including losses made ordinary by communicated special circumstances.

A person who fills an order addressed to someone else without disclosing the substitution acquires no contract with the buyer and cannot sue for the price, because the buyer intended to deal with the addressee.

A party claiming an express or implied contract to be paid for services must prove an actual mutual intention to contract, and services rendered within a family household are explained by the family relationship and do not by themselves imply a hiring.

A third person for whose benefit a promise is made, on valuable consideration moving from the promisee, may sue the promisor to enforce it, even though the third person was not a party to the agreement and furnished no consideration.
No contract is formed, and no action lies on a check given in the transaction, where both parties understood the whole exchange as a jest and neither intended the stated purchase and sale.

Where the nature of a contract makes the continued existence of a particular person or thing fundamental to performance, and its existence is not warranted, the law implies a condition excusing performance if that person or thing perishes without the contractor's default.

Where a contract term fits two different things because of a latent ambiguity and each party meant a different one, a shared name does not establish a shared referent, and the misunderstanding is a good answer to an action on the contract.

A reward offered to the finder of lost property is earned only by one who has a finder's possessory rights; a person who picks up an article its owner voluntarily laid down in a bank does not qualify.

Acceptance of an offer made between parties who are apart requires an appropriate outward act placed in a proper course of communication to the offeror; a private intention to accept, shown only by general preparations, is not enough.

A private act amending an insurer's charter will not be read as silently exempting that insurer from a general statute protecting insureds against avoidance for innocent misstatements; the two acts are harmonized.

A party who makes a positive, express promise must perform it despite unforeseen hindrance or hardship unless performance is prevented by an act of God, the law or the other party; difficulty short of absolute impossibility is no excuse.

A promise to keep an offer open that is unsupported by consideration does not bind the offeror, and the offeree cannot accept after learning that the offeror has agreed to sell the property to someone else.

Where a buyer expressly reserves the right to reject and decline to pay for a portrait that is not satisfactory to him, and the seller accepts those terms, the buyer's own dissatisfaction defeats the seller's claim to the price.

A party whose own conduct prevents or hinders the other's performance cannot rely on the resulting nonperformance, and parol evidence of surrounding circumstances may be used to show the contract's subject matter and that conduct.

Where a contract made by state officials for public advantage contains a provision expressly protecting an identified class, a member of that class may enforce the provision, including its stipulated damages, although not in privity with the contractor.

A letter quoting prices and inviting orders, without committing to sell any particular quantity, is a solicitation rather than an offer, so an order sent in response does not by itself form a contract.
Payment of part of a money debt already due, in the same manner, is not consideration for the creditor's promise to give up the rest, so the promise does not bind the creditor.

In a mercantile contract for goods to be shipped in stated monthly quantities, the time and amount of shipment are a condition precedent, and a materially deficient early shipment entitles the buyer to rescind the whole contract if the right is asserted distinctly and seasonably.

A completed sale of a specific article cannot be undone at law for mistake where both parties were ignorant of its true nature and value and the article delivered was the article sold; absent fraud, inadequacy of price alone gives no right to recover it.

A response to an offer that proposes different terms rejects the offer, and the offeree cannot afterward revive it by tendering an acceptance unless the offeror renews the offer or assents to the change.

A party's apparent assent may be avoided, before or after completion, when the bargain rests on a mutual mistake of material fact going to the substance of the thing bargained for, but not when the mistake concerns only its quality or an accidental attribute.

A party who responds to the other's apparent renunciation by electing to keep the contract alive remains bound to perform its own side, and proved expenses of preparing to perform are recoverable when lost profits are too speculative.
A promisee's surrender of a legal right at the promisor's request is sufficient consideration, even if the forbearance benefits the promisee and no benefit to the promisor is shown.

An oral contract to pay money after the promisor's death can be valid where a promise is given for a promise, and an offeror's immediate face-to-face assent to qualifications the offeree adds can produce agreement on the qualified terms.

A contract is severable when the consideration is apportioned among distinct performances, so the performing party may recover the stipulated price for each item fully performed, but nothing for an item only partly performed.

A statement of the lowest price at which a vendor would sell does not itself establish a contract to sell at that price to the person asking; the inquirer's reply agreeing to buy is only an offer requiring acceptance.

An advertisement promising a reward to anyone who performs stated conditions is an offer to the public that is accepted by performance, without advance notice of acceptance, and the requested performance supplies consideration.

Where prior dealings and a standing offer warrant a seller in sending conforming goods, the recipient's silence and retention of the goods for an unreasonable time can be found to be acceptance, because conduct importing assent counts as assent.

When an offer of guaranty invites an act that the offeror is unlikely to learn of promptly, the offeree must give notice of performance with reasonable diligence, and seasonably mailing a properly addressed, prepaid letter satisfies that requirement even if it never arrives.

A creditor's promise to hold a demand note only until he wants the money leaves him free to sue at once and so is no consideration for another's endorsement, and later actual forbearance does not cure an exchange intended as mutual promises.

A promisor who intentionally induces the promisee to change position for the worse in reasonable, foreseeable reliance on a gratuitous promise is equitably estopped from asserting lack of consideration.

Whether a price quotation is an offer depends on the whole exchange and its language, not its label; a quotation answering a specific inquiry and stated to be for immediate acceptance is an offer that the buyer's prompt order accepts.

Where a contract to do work on a building presupposes the building's continued existence and the building is destroyed without the worker's fault, further performance is excused and the worker may recover the fair value of the work done before the destruction.
A promise to perform the very services a person is already legally bound to perform for the promisor supplies no new consideration for the promisor's additional promise of payment.

Where a state of things assumed by both parties is the foundation of a contract, and an event that could not reasonably have been contemplated prevents performance of the substantial contract, the parties are discharged even though literal performance remains physically possible.

When a structure under repair is destroyed without either party's fault, both are discharged and the contractor may recover for labor and materials actually incorporated into the structure, but not for materials merely brought to the site.

Notice of the purpose for which goods are wanted does not make a seller liable for remote consequences not within the parties' contemplation when contracting, but a complaint alleging a contract and its breach is not dismissible merely because the damages demanded are unrecoverable.

A contract for personal property may be specifically enforced as freely as a land contract when the legal remedy is inadequate because of the contract's characteristic features or the parties' peculiar circumstances and needs, subject to equitable discretion.

A person who performs the act for which a private reward was offered cannot recover the reward unless he knew or had notice of the offer when he performed, because liability for the reward rests on contract.

The law imposes a quasi-contractual duty to pay reasonable compensation for necessary emergency professional services furnished in good faith to a helpless person, without actual assent or a successful outcome, but the fee may not be enlarged by the patient's wealth.

A seller who procures sales by secretly bribing the buyer's purchasing agent cannot recover the price, because public policy forbids enforcing contracts obtained through corruption of an agent, even if the buyer keeps the goods.

Contract damages must flow directly and naturally from the breach and be reasonably certain in nature and cause; telling a telegraph company a message's purpose does not make it liable for remote, speculative consequences.

An acknowledgment that an order has been received and will get prompt and careful attention is a promise to consider the order, not an acceptance of it, and its ordinary meaning is for the court to construe.

Where a contract gives a party a chance to compete for a prize, loss of that chance through breach is not too remote, and difficulty in valuing a contingent opportunity does not confine the injured party to nominal damages.
A contract carries an implied undertaking that neither party will intentionally prevent the other from performing, and a party who causes the other's nonperformance cannot rely on it as a defense.

A burglar's independent, voluntary criminal act breaks the causal chain between an alarm company's negligent failure of service and the theft, so the stolen property's value is not recoverable in tort, though damages for the breach of contract remain.

A promise to pay a fair share of profits is too indefinite to enforce where nothing identifies the share or a method of determining it, though one who has performed may seek the reasonable value of the services in quantum meruit.

When a contract conditions final payment on an architect's certificate, the architect's wrongful refusal to issue a certificate that has been earned excuses the condition, and the owner need not have participated in the refusal.

Where performance depends on the existence of a particular thing assumed as the basis of the agreement, performance is excused to the extent that thing does not exist, including where it can be obtained only by extraordinary means at prohibitive cost.

An offer that seeks acts rather than a return promise is accepted without words when the offerees enter upon the requested performance, and the offeror may not then defeat their interest while they continue performing as far as permitted.

As the Appellate Division held at this stage, an agreement granting an exclusive right is void for want of mutuality and consideration where the grantee's only promises depend on acts the writing does not require him to perform.

A promise addressed in substance to both parties to an existing contract, inducing them not to exercise their joint freedom to rescind or postpone it, is supported by consideration when they go on to perform.

Performance of a duty the promisee already owes under a contract with another person is not consideration for a third party's promise to pay for that performance, even if the third party gains financially.

A seller's mere knowledge that a buyer follows an unlawful occupation does not bar recovery of the price of an ordinary lawful article with legitimate uses, where the seller did not sell to aid that business or participate in an unlawful use.
Where a contract for work is entire and makes no provision about the time of payment, the contractor must substantially perform before payment can be demanded.

An owner who repeatedly makes payments without demanding the architect's certificate the contract requires cannot rely on the missing final certificate as a defense to payment for work honestly and substantially performed.

A promise to use reasonable efforts may be implied from an exclusive agency agreement read as a whole in its commercial setting, and that implied promise supplies consideration for the grant of exclusivity.

An owner who requires a contractor to build according to the owner's plans and specifications impliedly warrants that compliance will produce an adequate result, and general clauses requiring site inspection and plan checking do not negate that warranty.

A beneficiary may enforce a promise made on valid consideration for her direct benefit when the promisee's relationship to her falls within the principle of the close-family beneficiary cases; degree of kinship is not an absolute limit, and no pecuniary debt to her is required.

In a lengthy construction contract calling for progress payments, substantial compliance with the payment terms is a condition precedent to the contractor's duty to continue work, and a clause extending time for delay does not require the contractor to stand ready indefinitely.

An ordinary domestic arrangement between spouses living in amity, such as a promised allowance during a temporary absence, is not an enforceable contract unless the party asserting it proves a contract, expressly or by necessary implication, intended to have legal consequences.

Parties may mutually rescind an executory contract and at the same moment make a new one for the same performance at higher pay; the renewed mutual promises supply consideration, whereas a mere modification of a continuing contract needs new consideration.

A covenant restraining trade and personal liberty cannot be extended beyond its fair import, and where its words are unambiguous, extrinsic evidence of the parties' intentions is unnecessary and inadmissible.

A trivial and innocent departure from a construction contract does not forfeit the builder's right to the price but is compensated in damages, measured by diminution in value when the cost of replacement is grossly and unfairly disproportionate to the benefit.

An unconditional sale of specific goods in a deliverable state passes title when the contract is made, but a mutual mistake about a collateral fact existing at formation that materially induced the sale, such as a fire already threatening the goods, can permit rescission.

A buyer's competing purchases that merely make the seller's performance more difficult and expensive do not excuse the seller's breach; prevention excuses performance only where, as with an agreed exclusive source, the other party's conduct actually prevents it.

A gratuitous bailee who promises, as part of the bailment, to insure the goods and then receives them has entered on the undertaking and must perform that term; the bailment entered upon, not reliance alone, supplies the consideration.

An owner's occupancy of a building and delivery of a partial list of defects do not, as a matter of law, waive or estop proof of other defects; and a builder claiming substantial performance must explain departures from the contract and prove the allowance for them.

Where parties leave for future agreement both a price and the length of time that price will govern, a price ceiling alone does not complete the bargain; the court will not supply the missing duration, and the arrangement is an unenforceable agreement to agree.

An executory agreement that one party may cancel at any time lacks mutuality and is unenforceable as to future performance, and equity will not specifically enforce it at the suit of the party who holds the power to revoke.

When a writing is the complete agreement on a subject, an alleged prior or contemporaneous oral term that parties would naturally and normally include in that writing is barred by the parol evidence rule, even if sued on as a separate contract.

As this intermediate court reasoned before it was reversed, acceptance of an offer requesting a promise must be communicated unless the offeror dispenses with notice, and a letter merely acknowledging an order neither accepts nor gives that notice.

An offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance by authorizing a particular act as sufficient acceptance; the offeree then completes the contract by performing that specified act, without separately communicating it.

A seller's internal preparation to fill an order, such as referring it to the factory and incurring expense, is not acceptance; a buyer may cancel its order before acceptance is communicated or the goods are delivered.

A charity's acceptance of part payment on a pledge conditioned on a memorial to the donor implies a return promise to maintain and publicize the memorial, and that implied promise is consideration making the unpaid balance of the pledge enforceable.

A promisee who furnished consideration may sue in equity to enforce a promise to pay third-party beneficiaries, because his damages remedy at law is inadequate when nonpayment to them causes him no personal pecuniary loss.

A member of the public may sue on a contract between a municipality and its contractor only if the agreement shows an undertaking to make reparation directly to individual members of the public when the benefit is lost; a public benefit alone is incidental.

An oral agreement may be proved alongside a written contract only if it is collateral in form, does not contradict the writing's express or implied terms, and is one the parties would not ordinarily be expected to embody in the writing.

Specific performance of a long-term output contract for goods may be decreed where damages would be conjectural because future quantities and prices are uncertain and the goods, identified by their source, cannot readily be replaced.

When a physician guarantees a specified result, damages for breach are the difference between the value of the promised condition and the value of the actual condition, plus incidental consequences within the parties' contemplation, and not the pain ordinarily incident to the agreed operation.

After receiving an absolute repudiation, a contractor may not continue performing and charge the avoidable cost to the repudiating party; recovery is limited to labor, materials and expenses in partial performance before repudiation plus the profit the contract would have produced.

A seller is liable for the buyer's losses on resale contracts only if circumstances known to the seller at contracting made it reasonably foreseeable that its breach would cause the buyer to breach them; mere knowledge that the buyer is a wholesaler or intends resale is not enough.

On the casebook's account, an actor denied a promised engagement may lose more than salary, because billing and advertising that both parties knew would accompany the appearance are a valuable benefit of the contract itself.

Death excuses further performance of a personal-service contract but does not nullify the agreement, so a dispute over compensation for work already done arises under the contract and is within a broad arbitration clause that the personal representative may invoke.

A carrier with notice of the special purpose of a shipment is liable for the shipper's definite expenditures wasted by its delay, even though the shipper would have incurred those expenses had the carrier performed and cannot prove lost profits.
A statement of the minimum price below which an owner would not sell is not necessarily an offer; it may only open negotiations, and a purported acceptance of it forms no contract.

Naming a source of supply does not by itself condition a middleman's delivery obligation on the producer's willingness to produce enough; a seller that did not secure its supply bears the risk of the producer's voluntary reduction in output.

Evidence of a trade usage is admissible to show that parties in the trade used words or figures in a written contract with a special trade meaning, even though the terms appear unambiguous in their ordinary sense.

A general contractor's use of a supplier's quoted price in its own bid does not accept the supplier's offer, and promissory estoppel will not bind an offeror whose offer sought a return promise that was not given.

Caveat emptor does not bind parties who were honestly mistaken, in the essence of their bargain, about the identity of its subject matter, and a description of the goods in signed sale papers may operate as a warranty in law.

A moral obligation coupled with a material benefit actually received by the promisor, such as having his life saved, can support his later express promise to pay, even without a prior bargain or an original duty to pay.

A public reward offer may be revoked before acceptance by performance, but only in the manner in which it was made or by another method giving like publicity; private acts that convey nothing to the public do not revoke it.

Before a threat's effect on the particular person is measured, a legally qualifying threat must be shown; a threat to prolong civil litigation is not duress or menace, even if it actually induced the signature.
A job applicant's intentional concealment of background facts that are material to the employment, and that would have prevented the hiring if disclosed, vitiates the employment contract.

When a contractor deliberately fails to perform a construction obligation, the owner's damages are the reasonable cost of performing the promised work, even if that cost exceeds the value of the completed land; economic waste concerns only destroying a completed or substantially completed structure.
A contestant deprived of the chance to continue a winner-take-all contest cannot recover a share of the prize where it can be neither assumed nor proved that he would have won.

Parties to an existing contract may, in a single transaction, voluntarily rescind the old arrangement in whole or in part and substitute a fair new one, so an owner's voluntary surrender of his right to the original price is effective.

In an arm's-length sale of real estate, a seller's bare nondisclosure of a known hidden defect creates no liability absent a false statement, half-truth, active concealment, or a relationship imposing a duty to speak.

When a contract is frustrated, a party who paid in advance for future performance may recover the money in restitution if the consideration has wholly failed, that is, if the payer received none of the performance for which the payment was made.

Frustration of purpose discharges a promisor only if the frustrating event was not reasonably foreseeable and totally or nearly totally destroyed the value of the counterperformance; a regulation that merely makes a business less profitable does not excuse.
A humanitarian act voluntarily performed, even one that saves the promisor's life, is not sufficient consideration for the promisor's later promise to pay for the rescuer's injuries.

A bailee for hire relying on a liability limitation printed on a claim check must show reasonable notice of its terms and the bailor's assent; accepting a ticket issued to identify property does not establish that assent as a matter of law.

Temporary impossibility suspends a duty unless performance after it ends would impose a substantially greater burden, in which event the discharge is permanent; a specific clause leaving wartime obligations to future agreement controls inconsistent general provisions.

Specific performance of a contract for goods is available when the legal remedy is inadequate on the particular facts, but equity will withhold it from a party whose contract, taken as a whole, is too harsh and one-sided to enforce.

A promisee may recover necessary expenditures made in preparation for performance, but the promisor may reduce that recovery by any amount it proves the promisee would have lost had the contract been fully performed.

Damages for mental suffering are recoverable for breach of a personal contract so closely connected with the promisee's sensibilities that anguish from its breach is reasonably foreseeable, such as a contract to conduct a burial, without proof of a willful tort.

A promise to fabricate goods by a deadline with materials the customer will furnish ordinarily implies duties on the customer to supply those materials in time and to accept the finished goods without undue delay.

A buyer who keeps goods beyond a reasonable time without rejecting them cannot afterward rescind the sale for an innocent misrepresentation about a quality such as authorship; any remaining remedy is damages.

A promise requiring a particular person's services is excused when, without the promisor's fault, existing grounds reasonably indicate that performing would seriously endanger that person's life or health, even if performance remained physically possible and the fear later proves unfounded.

A party is estopped from asserting the statute of frauds where refusing enforcement would cause unconscionable injury to one who seriously changed position in reliance on the oral agreement, or would unjustly enrich one who accepted its benefits; no representation about a writing is required.

An offer unsupported by consideration is withdrawn when a communication reaching the offeree before acceptance states or implies that the offeror no longer consents to the transaction; no express words of revocation are required.

Parol evidence is admissible to show that a writing was not to take effect as a contract until a condition precedent occurred, unless the condition contradicts the writing or the writing expressly states that no outside conditions exist.

An order form requiring home-office acceptance can be accepted through correspondence: a letter promising attention to the order, together with a later letter cancelling that identified order, can evidence acceptance and recognize an existing contract.

A repudiating party's power to retract ends once the other party takes definite action treating the anticipatory breach as final, such as filing suit or firmly declaring that the breach will be accepted unless withdrawn within a stated period.

A statute of frauds memorandum may be pieced together from signed and unsigned writings that on their face refer to the same transaction, with oral evidence allowed to connect them and show assent, provided every essential term appears in the writings.

A contract freely made at arm's length without fraud is not void as against public policy merely because one party's return is large or the goods will ultimately be sold to the government; public policy must rest on identifiable law and precedent.

Contractual assent is judged by the reasonable meaning of a party's communicated words and acts, not by an unexpressed intention; a secret intent to jest is immaterial unless the other party knows of it.

An offer made face to face, with no time specified, ordinarily remains open only through the conversation, and conduct by the offeree that justifies the offeror in understanding the offer was rejected ends the power to accept.

Lost profits of a business not yet operating are ordinarily too speculative to recover for delay, unlike those of an established business with an operating history; delay damages may instead be measured by rental value and actual expenses.

Where an offer permits acceptance by commencement of performance, the offeree accepts by beginning performance within a reasonable time, and loading and dispatching materials and workers to the job can be commencement that precedes a later communicated withdrawal.

Anticipatory repudiation requires an absolute and unequivocal refusal to perform or a distinct and positive statement of inability; describing difficulty in obtaining materials and asking for help is not a repudiation.

Under an F.O.B. shipment contract the seller's obligation ends on delivery aboard the carrier at the named point, so a buyer's later inability to import the goods to its intended destination does not excuse acceptance and payment.

Forbearance to assert a claim that later proves invalid is sufficient consideration if the claimant honestly believed the claim valid and had an objectively reasonable basis for believing it possibly valid.

Although specific performance is ordinarily not the remedy for an agreement to sell personal property, equity may order delivery of a specific chattel when special circumstances give it a peculiar and unique value that makes damages inadequate.

A material breach can justify the injured party's repudiation, but a party who unilaterally treats the other's default as material and stops performing risks becoming the material breacher if that assessment proves unwarranted; materiality turns on several circumstances, not one mechanical test.

A public advertisement is an offer when it is sufficiently definite and leaves no further negotiation necessary to complete the transaction, and the advertiser may not impose new conditions after the offer has been accepted.

Exculpatory clauses are enforced unless settled public policy or the relationship of the parties counsels otherwise, and in 1958 Illinois applied that rule to uphold a residential lease clause relieving the landlord of liability for its own negligence.

Where the time of delivery is of the essence, the buyer's promised shipping instructions are also a condition of the seller's duty to deliver, and failure to give them in time discharges the seller's obligation.

Reasonable, foreseeable reliance producing a prejudicial change of position can support an implied subsidiary promise not to revoke an offer, making it irrevocable for a reasonable time even without bargained-for consideration.
A promise conditioned on the promisor's own satisfaction is not illusory, because the promisor must judge satisfaction honestly and in good faith, and that enforceable duty supplies consideration.

Rescission for a unilateral material mistake is ordinarily unavailable where the mistaken party failed to exercise ordinary diligence or where relief would seriously prejudice the other party beyond loss of its bargain.

A contracting officer's finding that the contract makes final and conclusive may be set aside for constructive fraud, which requires no actual dishonesty: a gross or arbitrary mistake amounting to a palpable substantial wrong is enough.

A contract whose separately priced preparatory steps exist only to secure a party's continuing readiness to perform is entire, not divisible, and that party's insolvency and assignment for creditors, disabling it from remaining ready, is a present total breach.
A builder who in good faith substantially performs a construction contract may recover the contract price less the reasonable cost of curing defects and omissions chargeable to the builder.

Between merchants, a written confirmation received and not objected to within ten days satisfies the UCC statute of frauds against the recipient; and, under this 1959 ruling, loss of goodwill was not recoverable as consequential damages for nondelivery.

After supervening impossibility, a subcontractor may recover the fair value of preparatory work the general contractor specifically requested under the contract, at least where the contractor contributed more to the impossibility and the work could not by its nature be wrought into the building.

A promise that the promisor should reasonably expect to induce definite and substantial action or forbearance, and that does induce it, is binding under Restatement (First) § 90 when injustice can be avoided only by enforcement, even without bargained-for consideration.
An arrangement among friends for a social outing does not manifest a bargained-for exchange and is not a contract, so a passenger on such a trip remains a guest under an automobile guest statute.

A bidder bound by an irrevocable bid may rescind for a material clerical mistake not resulting from neglect of a legal duty if enforcement would be unconscionable, the other party can be restored to the status quo, and the bidder rescinds promptly.

A party may be denied recovery on a contract lawful on its face when its performance involved gravely immoral and illegal conduct, such as commercial bribery, that is directly connected to the obligation sued upon and central to the performance.

Absent an express fee agreement, the law implies payment of the reasonable value of legal services, so a client or his estate may seek restitution of an advance exceeding the value of the services rendered, even if the client's own breach ended the representation.

Promises in a contract are presumed mutually dependent where possible, so a subcontractor's material breach of its promise of workmanlike performance justifies the contractor in withholding a progress payment, and the subcontractor cannot treat that justified withholding as a breach permitting it to stop work.

A party who asserts that an ambiguous contract term was used in the narrower of two possible senses bears the burden of proving that meaning, and a trade usage binds a newcomer only if actually known or so established that knowledge is chargeable.

A builder who substantially performs, judged by the essential purpose of the contract, recovers the contract price less damages for defects, measured by cost of repair for defects that can reasonably be corrected and by diminution in value where correction would cause unreasonable economic waste.

Intended will beneficiaries may sue the drafting attorney in negligence and as third-party beneficiaries despite lack of privity, but an attorney is not liable for an error on a legal question that competent lawyers may reasonably regard as doubtful.

A court of equity will not aid a plaintiff whose bad faith relates to the very transaction for which relief is sought, even if the defendant's conduct was also improper and the plaintiff's misconduct was not independently actionable.

An announced prize for a specified act is an offer for a unilateral contract, and performance with knowledge of the offer can accept it even if the performer did not act principally to obtain the reward.

A purchaser's deficient original tender does not bar specific performance where the vendor was already in default on title and the purchaser tenders performance in its equitable pleading and offers to pay whatever further sum the court finds due.

A c.i.f. sale that names no route is not frustrated when the customary route closes if a reasonable alternative route remains available at the time for shipment, even though it is longer and more expensive.
Parol evidence is admissible to prove an oral condition precedent to the legal effectiveness of a written agreement, provided the condition does not contradict the express terms of the writing.

Reasonable cost of performance ordinarily measures damages for omitted remedial work under a coal lease, but where the breached provision is merely incidental to the main purpose and the economic benefit of performance is grossly disproportionate to its cost, recovery is limited to diminution in value.

Evidence of negotiations is admissible to determine what an integrated writing means so long as the words can bear the proposed meaning, and a contract clause forbidding a court to use negotiations in interpreting the contract is void as against public policy.

A distributor may enforce, as a third-party beneficiary, another distributor's promise to the manufacturer not to sell outside its assigned territory when that promise primarily protects the other distributors and does not benefit them only incidentally.

Under Restatement (First) of Contracts § 90, a promise that foreseeably and actually induces definite and substantial reliance supports relief where injustice requires it, even if the promise lacks the terms needed for an enforceable contract.
A court may refuse to enforce a contract that was unconscionable when made, meaning that one party lacked meaningful choice and the terms unreasonably favored the other party.

Undue influence is excessive persuasion that overcomes a person's will by exploiting weakness or distress; it needs neither misrepresentation nor a confidential relationship, and consent so obtained may be rescinded.

Contract terms generally receive their ordinary meaning and technical terms their professional meaning; a term admitting varying meanings is construed strictly against the draftsman, and a provision restricting trade and land use is strictly construed.

Contractual intention is determined as of the time the agreement was made, and statutes then in effect become part of the contract, so a promise lasting until majority refers to the age of majority when the parties contracted.

An instrument diminishing legal rights that would otherwise exist, such as an exculpatory clause, is construed strictly against the party invoking it and must state the parties' intention with particularity.

Under the Indian Claims Commission Act, disparity in price alone establishes unconscionable consideration only where there is a very gross inequality, judged on each case's facts and circumstances and not by a mechanical percentage formula.

The clean-hands doctrine is discretionary and does not categorically bar enforcement of a professional football contract merely because the club agreed to keep the signing secret so a college player could appear in a postseason game.

A seller who promises delivery of a product it markets as a technological breakthrough assumes the risk that the breakthrough cannot be realized, and is not excused for impracticability under the standard of UCC section 2-615.

Receipt of a benefit and unjust retention are distinct requirements; quasi-contract cannot substitute a new debtor for the party with whom the plaintiff knowingly contracted and from whom it expected payment, absent mistake, direct dealings, or fraud.

Performance is excused for impossibility or commercial impracticability only if an unexpected contingency occurred, the risk of it was not allocated by agreement or custom, and the contingency made performance commercially impracticable; added expense alone did not suffice on this record.

When one transaction sells both goods and non-goods, Article 2 governs the sale of the goods even though non-goods predominate, so the seller cannot use the resale-price remedy for the goods without giving notice of a private resale.
When a sale of goods is unconscionable under UCC § 2-302 and the buyer keeps the goods, the seller recovers its net cost plus a reasonable profit and reasonable charges, not the contract price.

Mental weakness alone is not legal incapacity; the test is whether the person had sufficient reason to understand the nature and effect of the particular transaction, and a person with capacity who is vulnerable must prove fraud or overreaching.

The fairness of a contract and the adequacy of its consideration, for purposes of specific performance, are judged prospectively as of the time the contract was made, and a fair written contract to devise land is ordinarily specifically enforced.

Under UCC section 2-508(2), a seller who reasonably believed a nonconforming tender would be acceptable and who seasonably notifies the buyer of an intention to substitute conforming goods gets an opportunity to cure, which qualifies the buyer's right to reject for imperfect tender.

In computing lost profits for breach of contract, fixed overhead that the plaintiff would have borne whether or not the contract was performed is normally not deducted, because the breach did not save it.

Equity may reform a writing to match the parties' actual agreement where a term was omitted by mutual mistake, and one party's later denial does not prevent reformation when the mistake is shown by proper evidence such as that party's own conduct.

A building contractor whose defective work falls short of substantial performance may still recover in quasi-contract the amount by which the benefit conferred on the owner exceeds the owner's damages.

Punitive damages are not available for breach of contract, even a willful and malicious one, where no tort is pleaded or proved; and actual damages need not be proved with mathematical precision to support a modest compensatory award.

An attempt to negotiate additional terms does not terminate an option supported by consideration, because the option is itself a binding contract; the holder may still exercise it according to its terms within the option period.
Extrinsic evidence is admissible to interpret a written contract whenever it is relevant to a meaning the language is reasonably susceptible of, even if the writing appears clear on its face.

A court of equity ordinarily will not order specific performance of a construction contract where the order would be impractical to enforce and require supervising a complex project, absent special circumstances or direct involvement of the public interest.

Equity may refuse specific enforcement of a contract, though no sharp practice is shown, where the consideration is grossly inadequate and enforcement would impose oppressive hardship on the defendant out of proportion to the benefit to the plaintiff.

A party that gives one reason for terminating a contract is not confined to that reason unless the other party relied on it to its detriment; and a contractual notice period before termination does not by itself confer a right to cure.

A stipulated damages clause is enforceable liquidated damages, not a penalty, when at formation the harm was difficult to estimate, the parties made a reasonable effort to fix fair compensation, and the stipulated sum is reasonably related to probable damages.

Evidence of a collateral oral agreement is admissible unless the writing was intended as the complete embodiment of the bargain; a collateral term may be proved if similarly situated parties might naturally have made it separately and it does not contradict the writing.

The test for admitting extrinsic evidence to explain a written contract is not whether the writing appears plain on its face, but whether the offered evidence is relevant to prove a meaning to which the language is reasonably susceptible.

Statements framed as opinions may be actionable misrepresentations where the speaker has superior knowledge, a relationship of trust exists, the parties are unequally able to evaluate the subject, or a device makes the opinion misleading.

An employee whose suggestion is rejected under a program making a committee's decision final has no express contract claim, but may pursue unjust enrichment if the employer in fact used the idea, since a failed attempt to contract does not foreclose an obligation imposed by law.

A promise of one's own future conduct that is made to deceive, without intent to perform it, can support an action for fraud, each element of which must be proved by clear, cogent, and convincing evidence.

A buyer cannot justifiably rely on a seller's false representation when its falsity could have been discovered by ordinary observation during an ample opportunity to inspect, as distinct from a substantial investigation.

Plain contract language takes its ordinary meaning unless there is good reason to read it otherwise, and a party who first commits a substantial or material breach cannot invoke the other party's later refusal to perform as a ground to avoid the contract.

Preliminary negotiations may explain ambiguous contract language though they cannot vary plain terms, so a party told the other side's meaning before contracting is bound by it, while a party never told may rely on its own reasonable reading.
Dissolution of a partnership by one partner's withdrawal does not by itself terminate the firm's existing service contract where the firm's critical engineers remain available and able to perform.

A contract is voidable when mental illness or defect makes a person unable to act reasonably in relation to the transaction and the other party has reason to know of the condition, even if the person understood the transaction.

Even without an initial duty to volunteer information, a person who speaks on a subject must disclose the material facts needed to keep the communication from being deceptive; literal truth is not enough when fragmentary information creates a false overall impression.

To avoid a release for economic duress a party must show involuntary acceptance, no reasonably available alternative, and circumstances resulting from the other party's coercive conduct; its own financial difficulty or a disparity in size is not enough.

Under the California rule applied, anticipatory breach does not apply to a contract that is unilateral at inception or has become unilateral through one party's complete performance; the performing party must wait until the other's performance is due.

A wrongfully discharged employee recovers the agreed compensation less what the employer proves was or could reasonably have been earned in other employment, but only comparable or substantially similar work counts; different or inferior work need not be accepted.

A physician may contractually commit to a result, but recovery requires a specific, clear, express promise to cure or achieve a specified result, reasonably contemplated by both parties and relied upon by the patient; whether one was made is for the fact finder.

In an SEC enforcement action a court's general equity powers allow remedial relief beyond an injunction, including requiring insiders to give up profits from trading on undisclosed material information, so long as it is not a penalty.

A contract is read to give each term effect where possible, and under Maryland law a post-employment restraint must be reasonable and no broader than needed to protect the employer's business, such as customer relationships and confidential information.

A party ordinarily cannot rely on the nonoccurrence of a condition precedent when it has itself frustrated or prevented that condition, unless the other party's conduct is shown to justify the obstruction.

Under UCC §2-315, an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arises when the seller has reason to know the buyer's particular purpose and that the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment to select suitable goods.

A contract modification is voidable for economic duress when a party threatens to withhold goods owed under a contract, and the threatened party cannot obtain them from another source in time and an ordinary action for breach would be inadequate.

Under the UCC, evidence of trade usage and course of dealing is admissible to explain or supplement a written contract without a finding of ambiguity, unless it cannot reasonably be construed as consistent with the express terms or is carefully negated.

As the casebook reports the interim Richmond ruling, a seller facing a steep market rise was not wholly excused from its uranium supply contracts, though the judge was willing to hear argument for limiting the remedy.
An acceptance is expressly conditional under UCC § 2-207(1) only when it clearly conveys that the offeree will not proceed without the offeror's assent to the additional or different terms.

A condition precedent is an event the parties intend to occur before a right to performance arises, and when an express condition does not occur on its stated terms the conditional duty does not arise.

A party who knows the meaning the other party intends for an ambiguous term and accepts on that basis without communicating a different interpretation is bound by the known meaning, and the rule construing ambiguity against the drafter does not apply.

A service-station lease and dealer agreement form one franchise relationship, and public policy reads into it a restriction that the franchisor may not terminate, cancel or refuse to renew without good cause, meaning the dealer's failure substantially to perform.

A subcontractor who justifiably stops work after the other party's material breach may elect restitution for the reasonable value of the performance conferred, less payments received, without deduction for the loss it would have suffered by completing and without the contract price as a ceiling.

A patient may recover on a physician's clearly proved promise of a specific result even without negligence, and the damages may include out-of-pocket expenses, the worsening of the patient's condition, and pain and mental distress beyond what the promised treatment would have entailed.
Consideration need not move from the promisee: early payment of an employee's vested retirement share by a separate trust is a real benefit that supports his noncompetition promise to the employer.

A mixed contract for goods and services falls under Article 2 when its predominant factor, reasonably described, is a sale of goods with labor incidentally involved rather than the rendition of services with goods incidentally involved.
A seller who knows of a material latent defect not observable by the buyer and deliberately conceals or fails to disclose it may face rescission, even without any affirmative misrepresentation.

An employer's termination of an at-will employment contract that is motivated by bad faith or malice, or based on retaliation, is a breach of the employment contract, though damages for mental suffering are ordinarily not recoverable in a contract action.

A forward contract for a crop may be specifically enforced where a shortage makes the goods unique and irreplaceable, and a ginning cutoff date in such a contract carries an implied duty to harvest and gin in good faith.

A wrongfully suspended employee must seek other employment and the employer is credited with replacement earnings, but the employer bears the burden of proving both lack of reasonable diligence and the availability of suitable work.

A buyer faced with the seller's repudiation may cover by reasonable substitute purchases made in good faith and without unreasonable delay and recover the difference between cover cost and contract price plus incidental damages, without also proving market price.

Under UCC § 2-306 a seller's obligation under an output contract is measured by the output that actually occurs in good faith, so a seller may stop producing only in good faith, and merely earning less profit than expected does not justify cessation.

Where a contract expressly leaves the time of performance to later mutual agreement, the foreseeability of damages from delay is judged by what the breaching party knew when that date was fixed; reasonable costs of mitigating foreseeable harm are recoverable.

A party asserting impossibility must show that it took virtually every action within its power to perform; an impediment the party itself procured is no excuse, and a force majeure catchall is read in light of the listed events and the clause's purpose.

A contract to sell all the cotton a farmer grows on specified acreage is a definite, mutual and enforceable output contract, and a later dramatic rise in the market price does not make it unconscionable.

A party who agreed to a broad arbitration clause is bound by the arbitrators' determination that a damages clause is enforceable rather than a penalty, unless a public-policy question of sufficient magnitude warrants judicial intrusion.

A written "as is" exclusion of implied warranties under UCC §2-316(3)(a) satisfies the language requirement through commonly understood words but must still be conspicuous within the meaning of §2-316(2).

A requirements contract is valid under UCC § 2-306 because quantity is measured by good-faith requirements, and a seller invoking impracticability under § 2-615 must prove actual hardship from the contract and cannot rely on foreseeable business risks.

An acceptance must be definite and unequivocal; an acceptance made conditional on added terms is a counteroffer, but an acceptance accompanied by a request stands if it is clearly independent of whether the request is granted.

Where a licensing statute does not itself prescribe forfeiture of compensation, a court decides whether to add that civil consequence by weighing the whole transaction, including the centrality of the violation, the statute's policy, and the plaintiff's forfeiture against the defendant's gain.

A personal-service duty is discharged by operation of law when physical incapacity makes performance impossible or impracticable before it is due, and that excused nonperformance also discharges the other party's duties under the contract.

An attorney who drafts an estate plan owes a duty of ordinary care to its intended beneficiaries, who may sue for negligent drafting despite lack of privity, on a third-party contract or negligence theory.

A judge in urgent proceedings may order continued performance of a contract, backed by a daily coercive penalty, where a cost increase has not made performance materially impossible and the obligation continues through the contractual termination notice period.

A buyer may revoke acceptance when a nonconformity the seller fails seasonably to cure substantially impairs the goods' value to that buyer, measured by the buyer's own needs but proved by objective evidence, and the goods need not be useless.

A new business is not automatically barred from recovering lost anticipated profits; it may recover them if the evidence gives a reasonable basis for estimating the loss, without absolute or mathematical certainty, though the jury may not guess.

A school's catalog describing its admission criteria is an invitation to make an offer; tendering an application and fee is the offer, and the school's acceptance of them forms a contract to evaluate the application under the stated criteria.

The parol evidence rule does not bar proof of an oral promise made alongside a written agreement where the writing, viewed in its setting, does not integrate all the parties' promises and the oral promise is not one they would ordinarily have put in it.
Mental suffering caused by breach of contract is generally not recoverable; the few exceptions arise in fiduciary or quasi-fiduciary contractual relationships coupled with tortious conduct.

New York distinguishes certainty that damage exists from precision about its amount: where breach certainly caused some lost royalties on an existing recording, imperfect statistical proof of the amount is relevant, but further ventures depending on taste and fancy are too speculative.

As the assigned chapter reports it, the minimal nature of the difference between the work promised and the work done is irrelevant to whether the builder can be compelled to correct a departure from contractual specifications.

When an acknowledgment expressly conditioned on assent to additional terms goes unassented but both parties perform, UCC § 2-207(3) creates a contract consisting of the terms on which the writings agree plus supplementary Code terms, excluding the unagreed additional terms.

An ambiguous subcontract clause making final payment due after the owner pays the general contractor is construed as fixing a reasonable time for payment, not as a condition precedent; shifting the risk of owner nonpayment to the subcontractor requires unambiguous language.

Whether a communication is an offer depends on what a reasonable person in the recipient's position would understand from the words and conduct in their full setting, not on the sender's undisclosed intention; a price quotation can be an offer in light of prior dealings.

Economic duress exists where one party's wrongful conduct causes the other's involuntary assent in circumstances leaving no reasonable alternative; deliberately withholding an acknowledged debt from a party known to face bankruptcy can qualify.

Withholding a material truth can be equitable fraud justifying rescission when conscience and the circumstances impose a duty to speak, as when an applicant for a rabbinical position conceals a criminal conviction and disbarment.

A party's failure to read a clearly stated contract term printed in the same size type as the rest of the document does not establish mutual mistake for reformation or unfair surprise for unconscionability.

Even where a public-service contract intends some enforceable benefits for individual members of the public, a beneficiary suing in contract can recover only losses the promisor undertook to compensate or had reason to foresee as a probable result of breach.

Promissory estoppel does not require reimbursing negotiation expenses where the contemplated transaction was subject to contingencies that could have left those expenses unrecovered even had the promise been kept, because enforcement is then unnecessary to avoid injustice.

A modification of an existing contract, as distinct from an actual mutual rescission followed by a new bargain, requires new consideration; a price increase for land the seller is already bound to sell is unenforceable without it.
Unconscionability is evaluated as of the time the bargain is made, not in hindsight from the work eventually required or the result eventually achieved.

Under the clean-hands doctrine, equity will refuse to enforce a valid contract for a plaintiff whose misconduct is serious and sufficiently related to the transaction, including misconduct in which continuing the employment relationship necessarily involved the employee.

Absent a statute directing return of bribe money, a briber cannot recover it through the courts, whether the attempted corruption succeeded or failed, because agreements to commit a crime are illegal and void.

Property claims between knowingly unmarried cohabitants arising from a marriage-like relationship are unenforceable in Illinois because they conflict with the public policy implicit in the statutory marriage scheme, and any change is for the legislature.

A promisor that wrongfully prevents a condition from occurring cannot rely on its nonoccurrence to escape the promised performance, but conduct the contract authorizes, a risk the other party assumed, is not wrongful prevention.

Unless the parties agree otherwise, written notice exercising an option is effective only when the optionor receives it, so notice mailed on the last day of the term but received the next day is too late.

A merchant buyer's rejection of goods under a satisfaction clause is effective only if its dissatisfaction is genuine and in good faith, meaning honesty in fact and observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.

A party whose duty is conditioned on its own satisfaction is excused if it is genuinely dissatisfied with the subject of the condition, even though other motives also make the transaction unattractive, provided it made reasonable efforts to bring the condition about.

A breaching party cannot invoke the plaintiff's failure to mitigate when the defendant had the primary contractual duty to perform, an equal opportunity to take the same preventive step, and equal knowledge of the consequences.

When lost property has neither a market value nor a means of replacement or reproduction, damages are measured by its actual or intrinsic value to the owner, which may reflect ordinary attachment but excludes unusual sentimental or fanciful value.

A motorist's beneficiary rights under particular clauses of a roadside-service contract do not extend to consequential personal-injury and death damages that fall outside the responsibility the contracting parties contemplated.

A promise to use best efforts to promote and maintain a high volume of sales does not require the promisor to incur bankruptcy or substantial losses, but it is not discharged by pursuing overall profit while disregarding the promised volume.
A clearly disclosed franchise provision permitting termination without cause on reasonable notice is not inherently unconscionable, and exercising it openly is not by itself bad faith.

A purchaser of land whose breach was not willful may recover payments to the extent the seller is unjustly enriched, but bears the burden of proving the seller's damages were less than the money retained, and a ten percent liquidated-damages clause is presumptively reasonable.

A court may equitably modify the price term of a long-term contract when a mutual mistake about the capacity of a negotiated price index, or resulting impracticability or frustration, causes severe loss beyond the bounded risk the disadvantaged party assumed.

An at-will employee states a tort claim for wrongful discharge when he alleges that he was dismissed for a demonstrably improper reason that contravenes a clear mandate of public policy, such as insisting on compliance with a statute.

A store advertisement stating a sale price is an invitation to negotiate rather than an offer a shopper can accept, although a materially misleading advertisement may still give rise to statutory liability without proof of intent to deceive.

Under Restatement section 90 an employer whose definite job offer foreseeably induces a person to resign from existing employment may be liable for that person's reliance losses, even though the promised employment would have been terminable at will.

A material false representation of existing or past fact is actual equitable fraud that supports rescission without proof of knowing falsity or quantified monetary loss, and the wrongdoer cannot defend by saying the victim should have investigated.

Under the UCC, specific performance is available when goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, such as when a substitute cannot readily be obtained; and an accepted part payment satisfies the statute of frauds for an oral sale of one indivisible item.

A contract of adhesion is enforceable unless a term falls outside the adherent's reasonable expectations or is unduly oppressive or unconscionable; an arbitration clause naming a body whose interests are effectively identical to one party's as sole arbitrator will not be enforced.

Under the UCC, trade usage and course of performance are part of the parties' agreement and may qualify an express term, such as a posted-price term, so long as they can reasonably be construed as consistent with it, without any showing of ambiguity.

A seller that has accepted orders and then unequivocally refuses to perform them after receiving adequate assurances commits anticipatory repudiation; it cannot unilaterally rescind its acceptances, and ending a continuing relationship for future orders does not discharge orders already accepted.

A pension promise made after an employee has independently decided to retire is not supported by bargained-for consideration and is not enforceable by promissory estoppel, because the promise did not induce the retirement or other forbearance.

The intent embodied in a clear written agreement is found in its expressed terms; a court will not use extrinsic evidence or its own view of fairness to rewrite unambiguous language, and ambiguity cannot be manufactured by an unreasonable alternative construction.

A landlord who accepts late rent for years without objection may waive the right to treat that lateness as a default despite a lease clause requiring written waivers, and equity may relieve a tenant from forfeiture of a purchase option for defaults that have been cured.

An express warranty requires that the seller's affirmation become part of the basis of the bargain through the buyer's reliance, and consequential damages for its breach require separate proof that the breach caused each particular loss.

Under UCC section 2-714(2), damages for accepted goods are the difference between their value as accepted and the value they would have had as warranted; the contract price is relevant evidence of warranted value but is not controlling.

Rescission for mutual mistake requires a mistaken belief about an existing fact that relates to a basic assumption and materially affects the agreed performances, and it is unavailable to a party who bears the risk of the mistake, as under an acceptance-of-present-condition clause.

Under Indiana law, the parties to a contract for a third party's benefit may rescind or vary it, without having expressly reserved that power, at any time before the beneficiary accepts, adopts or acts on it.
A third-party beneficiary remains subject to defenses against the underlying agreement, so a beneficiary's claim under an oral premarital agreement is barred by the Statute of Frauds.

When an agreement between spouses is too indefinite to enforce, a spouse who made an extraordinary, unreciprocated contribution to the other's education under it may recover in restitution, measured by her financial contribution and capped by the benefit she expected.
A contract term may be unenforceable as against public policy when it conflicts with a strong policy shown by a statute's purpose, history and scheme, even if no statute expressly prohibits the term.

Definite handbook provisions, such as disciplinary procedures, distributed to an at-will employee can become a binding unilateral contract when the employee keeps working with knowledge of them, the continued service supplying both acceptance and consideration.

The detriment required for promissory estoppel is not measured only by comparing financial gains and losses; forgone alternatives and nonfinancial burdens assumed in reliance on the promise can make the reliance substantial, and whether they do is a question of fact.

In Maryland, when a commercial transaction sells consumer goods that retain that character after performance and monetary loss or personal injury arises from a defect in them, implied warranties apply to those goods even though consumer services predominate.
A general contractor's use of a subcontractor's price and listing of that subcontractor in its successful prime bid does not, without more, manifest acceptance of the subcontractor's offer.

Where a statute prescribes a parent's written consent as the means of authorizing use of a minor's image, a consent that meets the statute binds the child, who cannot later disaffirm it under the common-law infancy rule.

A settlement cannot be set aside for economic duress merely because the claimant badly needed money and the other side refused to raise its offer; financial distress not caused by the other party does not make a facially reasonable compromise voidable.

Whether a best-efforts obligation requires exclusivity depends on the circumstances, including trade usage; a distributor breaches it by taking on a directly competing product where doing so would necessarily dilute the promised effort.

Damages for breach of a promise to deliver stock under an option are the stock's market value at the time of the breach less the exercise price, and an issuer's earlier repudiation does not fix the breach date if the holder keeps the option alive.
A brokerage agreement that entitles the broker to a commission at the time of closing makes closing a condition precedent, so no commission is owed if the purchaser defaults before closing.

Efforts made in negotiating a deal that are ordinary attempts to secure one's own business advantage, conferring at most an incidental benefit on the other side, do not support recovery in unjust enrichment.

An oral agreement is within the one-year provision of the statute of frauds only if its terms make full performance within a year impossible; the possibility that it will end within a year through breach does not count as performance.
Under Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 211, a standardized term is not part of the agreement if the drafter has reason to believe the adhering party would not assent if aware of it.

Under UCC section 2.601 a buyer may reject goods that fail to conform to the contract in any respect, but conformity is measured by the parties' actual agreement and the right to reject must be exercised in good faith.

A buyer's market-price damages for nondelivery may be limited to its actual lost resale profit where the seller knew of the resale contract, the buyer has not shown liability to its own customer, and the seller did not breach in bad faith.

A business buyer's promise to the seller to pay the seller's listed debts makes each listed creditor an intended beneficiary of a new, separate obligation, and limitations on a debt not yet barred when assumed runs from the new undertaking, not the original maturity.

An insurance contract for the benefit of an unnamed third party may be implied at law when that party belongs to the class of beneficiaries the coverage contemplated and recognizing it does not change the insurer's risk.

Persons expressly designated in a public contract as the consumers the promisor undertakes to serve are intended third-party beneficiaries, even though they buy from the promisee rather than directly from the promisor.

Under former Civil Code article 1184, a party whose counterparty has not performed may compel performance when it is possible, so a court may not refuse conformity with a contractual specification without investigating whether restoring conformity is impossible.

A contract right cannot be assigned where assignment would materially increase the obligor's burden or risk; an indemnity right cannot be assigned to a party whose substitution materially increases the likelihood that the indemnitor will have to pay.

An acceptance must be absolute, unequivocal and unconditional and must express an intention to form the contract by that response; a reply that shows readiness to proceed but leaves a material term open is not an acceptance.

A promise is not illusory, and supplies consideration, when the promisor surrenders a legal freedom he otherwise had, even if reserved powers and contingencies may reduce the practical value the promisee receives; the existence of consideration is distinct from its adequacy.

A public reward offer can be accepted only within its own terms and while it remains open; a later news report replaying the offer does not renew it, and ratification cannot supply legal significance the replayed act itself lacks.

A parent or relative who executes an instrument under threats of, and in fear of, criminal prosecution of a child or relative may avoid it for duress, and bringing an equitable action for cancellation is itself sufficient disaffirmance.

A seller of a home must disclose material facts that the seller knows or should know and that the buyer could not discover through ordinary care and diligence; breach of that duty is constructive fraud supporting rescission.

A home seller who knows of facts materially affecting the property's value that are not readily observable and are unknown to the buyer must disclose them, and the duty applies to new and used property alike.

A writing may be reformed to the innocent party's understanding where that party's unilateral mistake coincides with the other party's fraud, and a failure to read does not bar relief when the other party's trick induced it.

Where a contract excludes consequential damages, recovery for breach of a service promise is limited to the direct loss, the difference between the value of the services promised and the value of those supplied; resulting property damage is consequential even if foreseeable.

Under this district-court ruling, which the First Circuit later rejected, consequential contract damages for career harm that depends on others drawing a message from a cancellation require proof of an unprivileged, materially false communication, by analogy to defamation law.

A promise that can be performed by alternative methods is not discharged because one becomes impracticable while the other remains practicable; but a clause adjusting minimum purchases when the buyer is unable to receive is triggered by impracticability, not only absolute impossibility.

Under UCC §2-313, a seller's affirmation of fact or description creates an express warranty without formal words or intent to warrant, and it is presumed to be part of the basis of the bargain unless the seller proves otherwise.

A party whose option or right of first refusal is repudiated need not tender performance, but to recover damages he must prove that he would have been ready, willing and able to perform within the option period.

Under Illinois law a liquidated damages clause must be a reasonable estimate, at formation, of likely damages that are difficult to measure; a formula awarding unearned gross revenue without deducting the costs the promisee avoids is an unenforceable penalty.

Consideration may be a benefit to the promisor or a detriment to the promisee, so listening to a radio station because of its promised reward can be consideration for the station's promise even though the listener pays nothing.

Where parties intend not to be bound until a formal writing is executed no contract arises from their oral dealings, but one whose services were designed to benefit the other side, and did enrich it, may recover in unjust enrichment.

The parties' later discussions and conduct are strong evidence of what they understood their contract to require, and a claimed trade usage is tested in the particular market where the transaction occurred and must be shown by regular observance.

Unconscionability under UCC § 2-302 can apply between merchants; the primary consideration is the substantive reasonableness of the term, and unequal bargaining power alone will not invalidate a reasonable provision.

When a contract requires written notice within a stated period, the writing must actually be received within that period; and under New York law a seller of real estate may retain a traditional ten percent down payment when the buyer defaults without excuse.

A real-estate broker is entitled to the commission, even under a rule that ordinarily requires the sale to close, when the seller's own conduct prevents completion of a sale to a buyer the broker produced who was willing and able to perform.

Lost profits are recoverable only if the breach caused them, they are proved with reasonable certainty and are not speculative, and they were fairly within the parties' contemplation when contracting; a new enterprise faces stricter scrutiny.

Illness of an employee discharges a contractual duty only if the parties understood performance to depend on that particular person's services; if another can perform without violating the contract, the promisor's own inability or added cost is no excuse.

Specific performance rests in judicial discretion; physical uniqueness does not compel it, because the question is whether the promised interest can be valued reliably enough for damages to be adequate, and relief may also be denied where it would impose disproportionate hardship.

Force majeure, impossibility, impracticability and frustration cannot shift back a risk the contract expressly assigns; a buyer bound to a fixed quantity and price floor bears the risk of a market decline, including one operating through government economic regulation.

Under UCC § 2-210(1), the duty of performance under an exclusive distributorship cannot be delegated without the obligee's consent to a competitor of the obligee or to the competitor's wholly owned subsidiary.

A seller who has performed does not ordinarily lose the right to payment merely because the buyer plans an improper use of the goods, but a seller who acts to further that improper use may be denied enforcement on public-policy grounds.
