An express agreement to negotiate in good faith is enforceable, even though the ultimate contract is unfinished, if the parties manifested an intent to be bound by it, its terms are sufficiently definite, and it is supported by consideration.

Good-faith forbearance from asserting a claim that later proves invalid can be consideration if the claim was objectively doubtful or the surrendering party honestly believed it might fairly be determined valid.

A contract is voidable for mutual mistake about a basic assumption material enough to upset the exchange, but absent fraud or misrepresentation the rescinding party recovers only restitution of benefits conferred, not consequential damages for reliance expenditures.

An advertisement that requests a specified performance without further communication is an offer of a unilateral contract, and the bargained-for act is consideration regardless of equivalence of values, but the offeree must give reasonable notice of performance when the offeror could not otherwise learn of it.

Under New York law parties who contemplate a later formal writing are bound beforehand if their objective manifestations show intent to be bound, judged by any express reservation, partial performance, agreement on essential terms, and whether such a deal is ordinarily put in writing.

A misrepresentation can make assent voidable if it is either fraudulent or material, and a buyer's cover under the UCC must be a good-faith, timely purchase of reasonable substitutes that serve the intended commercial use.

A representation about the legal effect of a document is ordinarily a nonactionable opinion, and it does not support fraud between equally sophisticated parties dealing at arm's length with equal access to legal advice.
A court will refuse to enforce an exculpatory clause as a matter of law when it is printed so that the customer cannot read it, apart from any question of unconscionability.

A sale may be annulled for mistake about a substantial quality when the sellers consented in the firm conviction that a painting could not be by a particular artist while that attribution in fact remained possible.

Foreseeability of a supervening event is not an absolute bar to the defense of impossibility; it is evidence bearing on whether the event was sufficiently likely that the promisor should have guarded against it or bore its risk.

Impossibility excuses performance only when destruction of the subject matter or means of performance makes it objectively impossible through an event that could not have been foreseen or guarded against in the contract; a force majeure catchall reaches only events of the kind listed.

Performance is excused for impossibility or commercial impracticability when an unexpected intervening occurrence, whose nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the agreement, makes performance impracticable without the promisor's fault and no reasonable alternative exists.

A seller who resells is not confined to UCC section 2-706 and may recover lost profit under section 2-708(2) by proving it is a lost-volume seller: it had capacity for both sales, both would have been profitable, and it probably would have made the second sale anyway.

Services performed gratuitously, without expectation of payment, are past consideration and cannot support a later promise to pay for them; a promise made because assistance has already occurred, rather than to procure it, is unenforceable for lack of consideration.
Advertisements and general sales solicitations ordinarily invite offers; a customer's order sent in response is itself the offer, and no contract is formed until the seller accepts it.

The at-will presumption may be rebutted by an implied-in-fact agreement to discharge only for good cause, but breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing in an employment contract does not give rise to tort remedies.

Family pressure, persuasion and the emotional difficulty of the choice do not amount to duress that lets a natural parent revoke a consent to adoption, at least where she knew of and rejected other options.

Contract damages for specific, identifiable employment opportunities lost because of a breach are recoverable if they satisfy the ordinary requirements of natural consequence, foreseeability and reasonably certain proof, and are not barred as general reputation damages.

Under Swiss Code of Obligations article 163(3), a judge reduces a contractual penalty only when it exceeds what is reasonable and compatible with law and equity, and the debtor must assert and prove the conditions for reduction.

A paid surrogacy contract that binds the mother before birth to surrender the child and terminate her parental rights is illegal and unenforceable as contrary to adoption statutes and public policy; custody is decided by the child's best interests.

Under UCC § 2-716, specific performance is available for unique goods or in other proper circumstances, but it remains inappropriate where money damages are available and adequate; a higher replacement price alone does not justify it.

Under California law as stated in Pacific Gas & Electric, a party must be allowed to offer extrinsic evidence that an integrated contract means something other than what it appears to say, even where the writing seems clear on its face.

An employer may change a generally applicable written discharge-for-cause policy to at-will employment without having reserved the right to do so, provided reasonable notice of the change is uniformly given to affected employees.

At-will employment is a rebuttable construction of unspecified-duration arrangements, and an employment manual and surrounding circumstances can create an implied-in-fact contract term limiting discharge, without separate consideration or symmetrical termination rights.

A contract is voidable for mental incapacity if the person cannot reasonably understand the nature and consequences of the transaction, or cannot act reasonably in relation to it and the other party has reason to know of the condition.
Accepting an assignment of rights under a contract is analytically distinct from undertaking the assignor's existing duties under it, such as its unpaid debts to the other party.
The beneficiary of a life insurance policy has the contractual and statutory relationship with the insurer needed to claim breach of the insurer's duty of good faith.
As the assigned chapter reports it, a seller who supplies goods that do not conform to the contractual specification may be ordered to perform the sale contract by replacing them.

A buyer's order inviting prompt shipment may ordinarily be accepted by the seller's shipping conforming or nonconforming goods, but under UCC § 2-206(1)(b) a nonconforming shipment seasonably identified as an accommodation is a counteroffer, not an acceptance.

Unusual or extraordinary damages are recoverable only if liability for them was contemplated at or before contract formation as a probable consequence of breach, judged by the contract's nature, purpose and circumstances and the liability the defendant consciously assumed or reasonably led the plaintiff to believe it assumed.
Whether a contract forms when a service appointment is scheduled, or only when performance begins, is a question of fact that cannot be assumed; an appointment may be only an invitation to negotiate.
A buyer who notifies the seller may withhold or deduct from the price due damages resulting from the seller's material breach of the same contract, even after accepting the goods.

A subcontract provision conditioning payment on the owner's payment is construed by the court as a matter of law: if unambiguous it is a condition precedent, and if ambiguous it merely fixes a reasonable time for the general contractor to pay.

Under the UCC, a buyer may recover lost profits as consequential damages for breach of warranty, including secondary profits where the nonconforming good is a primary product and cover is unavailable; goodwill damages are no longer barred as a matter of law.

Prenuptial agreements are evaluated as ordinary contracts and bind the parties absent fraud, misrepresentation or duress, without judicial review of their reasonableness, provided there was full and fair disclosure of the parties' financial positions.

When parties intend to remain bound by a long-term contract and the agreed mechanisms for setting the price fail, a court may supply a reasonable price supported by the evidence and may order continued performance where future damages would be too speculative.

A complete, clear and unambiguous written contract is enforced according to its terms, and extrinsic evidence of what the parties intended may not be used to create an ambiguity in it or to add to or vary it.

Under Pennsylvania's Chanoff v. Fiala, where use of the mail is authorized or implied, posting an option exercise completes it, although the general rule recognized by the court is that an option exercise takes effect on receipt.

Under UCC 2-207 an additional term in an acceptance between merchants that materially alters the bargain, meaning one to which consent cannot reasonably be presumed, does not become part of the contract unless the other party actually consents to it.

A party that satisfies a contract's express terms may still be liable in contract damages for breaching the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing if it deliberately acts to destroy the other party's contractual benefits for its own advantage.

After the other party's repudiation, a party may stop performing and sue for total breach or continue the contract and sue for partial breach; having elected to continue and keep the benefits, it may not withhold its own material performance.

Where a contract has no forfeiture or liquidated-damages clause, a defaulting buyer is entitled under Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 374(1) to restitution of the part of a deposit that exceeds the seller's actual damages, and bears the burden of proving the excess.

A seller recovers lost profit as a lost-volume seller by proving capacity for both sales, that the additional sale would have been profitable, and that it probably would have been made absent the breach.

An injured party that has performed all of its contractual duties cannot obtain restitution in quantum meruit when all that remains due from the other party is payment of a definite sum; the agreed price is the measure.

Loss of future business with a known customer may be a foreseeable consequence of delivering seriously defective goods, but lost future profits are recoverable only to the extent their amount is proved with a fair degree of certainty rather than by speculation.

Under Michigan law as the Sixth Circuit applied it, a market downturn and a party's own financial losses are not the failure of a basic assumption, so neither impracticability nor frustration excuses a manufacturer that ends a dealer agreement without following its agreed termination procedures.

An assignment is effective when the assignor manifests intent to transfer the right and relinquishes control and power of revocation; an obligor with notice who pays the assignor instead is liable to the assignee.

Under Connecticut's one-year statute of frauds provision, an oral contract that does not expressly prescribe a duration beyond one year is treated as of indefinite duration and falls outside the provision, however long performance will actually take.

Under Illinois common law, in-house counsel generally cannot bring a retaliatory-discharge tort claim against the employer-client, because the public policy at stake is protected by the lawyer's mandatory professional duties.

A party's remaining duties are discharged when, without its fault, a supervening event substantially frustrates its principal purpose and the event's nonoccurrence was a basic assumption of the contract, unless the language or circumstances allocate that risk to the party.

A forum-selection clause in a non-negotiated form passage contract is enforceable under federal admiralty law if it is reasonable and survives judicial scrutiny for fundamental fairness; lack of negotiation alone does not make it unenforceable.

Under promissory estoppel, a promise of a continuing at-will relationship cannot support recovery of expected future profits, but it can support reliance damages for an existing opportunity the promisee foreseeably surrendered in reliance on it.
The duty of good faith in performance does not require altruism or general candor, but it forbids deliberately exploiting the other party's oversight about its rights under the existing contract.

Contract damages ordinarily compensate the injured party's own loss; the breaching party's gains can sometimes help measure that loss, but gains that do not correspond to it are not automatically recoverable in an ordinary contract action, and a supported estimate of the loss suffices despite uncertainty.

Under Indiana promissory estoppel a conditional promise can be enforced where the promisor should reasonably have expected the general nature and extent of the reliance it induced, with recovery limited to reliance damages.

An employee claiming an agreement that alters presumptive at-will employment must prove by clear and convincing evidence a promise with ascertainable, definite terms; general assurances of job security are not enough.

A minor who disaffirms a fair purchase made without overreaching, after paying money and using the article, may recover the price only subject to the seller's reasonable compensation for use, depreciation, and willful or negligent damage.

Under the Sixth Circuit's prediction of Michigan law, application fraud discovered after discharge can supply just cause for the discharge if the misrepresentation was material, directly relevant to evaluating the candidate, and relied upon in hiring.

Contract damages are limited to probable consequences of breach that were reasonably foreseeable when the contract was made; proof that a discharge caused a continuing psychiatric disability does not show the employer should have foreseen it at hiring.

When a seller anticipatorily repudiates, the buyer's market-price damages under UCC section 2-713 are measured at the date of repudiation if cover then would be commercially reasonable; otherwise the buyer may wait a commercially reasonable time, and bears the burden of showing why immediate cover was unreasonable.

When a seller repudiates and the buyer does not cover, the buyer may recover the market-price/contract-price difference under UCC section 2-713 even if that exceeds the buyer's actual lost profit; the specific damages provision controls over the Code's general compensatory principle in section 1-106.

A promise that is not enforceable as a conventional contract may still be enforced under promissory estoppel when it is clear, induces intended and actual detrimental reliance, and must be enforced to avoid injustice; the First Amendment does not bar applying that generally applicable doctrine to the press.

A permanent injunction against breach of contract is proper when the plaintiff shows that damages are an inadequate remedy, which the court decides by comparing the costs and benefits of damages and injunctive relief in the particular case.

Where an offeror seeks actual performance rather than a return promise, the offeree's completed performance accepts the unilateral offer and supplies the bargained-for detriment, even though the offeree was free to withdraw before completing it.

Promissory estoppel requires an actual, clear and definite promise that induces reasonable reliance; expressions of expectation, statutory eligibility representations, and corporate promotion made in seeking a tax abatement are not such a promise.

Under Pennsylvania law as described in this decision, a minor's contracts other than for necessaries are voidable, and shelter is not invariably a necessary; it depends on the minor's situation and whether a parent or guardian is able and willing to supply it.
A spouse's personal nursing care of an ill spouse falls within the existing marital duty of support, so a promise to compensate that care lacks new consideration and is contrary to public policy.

A creditor taking a wife's security for her husband's debts is put on inquiry, and unless it takes reasonable steps to see that her consent is properly obtained it has constructive notice of any misrepresentation or undue influence by the husband.

A usage of trade can modify or exclude an implied warranty without actual knowledge, binding those in the trade or who should be aware of it; where buyer and seller are in different trades, the seller must show the buyer knew or should have known.

A party breaches the implied duty of good faith in every contract when it knowingly exploits its contracting partner's mistake during performance, as distinct from merely remaining silent or having superior knowledge.

An agreement among law partners imposing a reasonable, geographically limited financial cost on a departing partner who competes is not automatically void under California's rule against restricting a lawyer's practice, but an absolute ban or a disproportionate charge is unenforceable.

A shipowner cannot treat a classification society's certificate as a guarantee of the vessel's sound construction; the owner keeps its nondelegable duty of seaworthiness, and a great disparity between the fee and the loss claimed suggests the parties did not allocate that risk to the society.

Under UCC section 2-207, a buyer's added form term is excluded where the seller's offer barred changes or the contract arose only from conduct, and a buyer whose seller was not told of the downstream use assumes the risk that its own customer cannot perform.

A seller that complies in good faith with informal governmental requirements barring performance establishes commercial impracticability under UCC section 2-615; it need not defy the government before claiming excuse.

Under the 1993 approach, later reversed, a promisor under a unilateral promise of sale owes only an obligation to act until the option is exercised, so withdrawal before exercise prevents the sale from forming and bars compelled completion.

A contractual duty to negotiate in good faith, read as honesty in fact, forbids trickery but does not require concessions, disclosure of one's reservation price or strategy, or giving up commercial advantages the contract allocates.

A minor's contract is voidable, but after reaching majority the former minor ratifies it by failing to disaffirm within a reasonable time or by a distinct, decisive act clearly showing affirmation, and a ratified contract can no longer be avoided.

As the federal court predicted New Jersey law, a gambler has no dram-shop tort claim against a casino for losses incurred while intoxicated, but intoxication so complete that he could not appreciate the nature and consequences of his act remains a contract defense to the casino's credit claim.

Fraudulent concealment requires a duty to disclose a material fact, concealment or nondisclosure, induced action or inaction, and resulting damage, so proof that a seller hid a report fails without substantial evidence that the concealment induced the purchase and caused damage.

A court may reform an executed writing that fails to express the parties' agreement because of mutual mistake, and a party's failure to discover the mistake does not bar reformation unless it amounts to a lack of good faith and fair dealing.

A rent-to-own agreement that transfers ownership after a series of payments for no further consideration is in substance a credit sale and security transaction, and charging disguised interest above the statutory limit is an unconscionable commercial practice.

An in-house lawyer may sue the employer for breach of an implied-in-fact promise to discharge only for good cause, and may bring a limited public-policy retaliatory-discharge tort, so long as the claim can be established without breaching the attorney-client privilege.

An employee may recover for intentional infliction of emotional distress connected with a discharge only when the distress results from an outrageous manner of carrying out the discharge, not from the fact of the discharge itself.

Where the cost of remediating land to a contractual standard is grossly disproportionate to the resulting economic benefit, damages for breach of the promise to remediate are capped at the diminution in the property's value.

An employee suing a former employer for tortious interference with a new job need not accept reemployment from that employer to mitigate, and an offer of reemployment reduces recovery only if it does not require renewed association that circumstances make offensive or degrading.

A grantee who accepts a deed is bound by its mortgage-assumption clause even without signing it, and that promise to the grantor is an original undertaking, not a promise to answer for another's debt within the suretyship statute of frauds.

A party who assents to a patently ambiguous term accepts the risk of an authorized tribunal's construction of it; misunderstanding prevents a contract only where no sensible, nonarbitrary basis selects between the parties' understandings.

Under the majority knockout rule, which the court predicted Illinois would adopt for UCC section 2-207, conflicting terms in an offer and an acceptance that is not expressly conditional cancel each other out, and the Code's gap-filling provisions supply the term.

A stipulated damages clause is enforceable if it is reasonable under the circumstances as a fair estimate of compensation; in commercial contracts between parties of comparable bargaining power it is presumptively reasonable, and the challenger bears the burden of showing it is unreasonable.

A contract that is lawful on its face is not unenforceable merely because it arose from an antitrust conspiracy; enforcement is refused only if the judgment would itself enforce the precise conduct the antitrust laws prohibit.
In Massachusetts a charitable pledge is enforceable only if there is a promise to transfer property for a charitable purpose and that promise is supported by either consideration or reliance.

An express contract bars quasi-contractual recovery only on the subject matter it covers, so a party may recover in quantum meruit for a distinct benefit the contract left unaddressed, or where a contractual waiver was induced by fraud and is avoided.

On the quoted Nebraska reasoning, a minor's position on disaffirmance is not defeated because services received cannot be returned; the resulting loss falls on the adult, to discourage adults from contracting with minors.

Contract terms are read in the context of the whole instrument, and a word with alternative dictionary meanings is not ambiguous where the contract's other provisions resolve its meaning; extrinsic evidence is resorted to only for ambiguity.
Whether an attorney's fee is unconscionable depends on the value of the services to the client measured against the market for comparable lawyers, not on the law firm's cost or profit margin.

Continued employment after a fixed-term contract ends, without objection or a new arrangement, can imply a renewed contract on the prior terms, and a competition-payment clause was enforced after a discharge under a cause definition that included homosexuality, the two affirming judges giving different reasons.

A contractually designated architect's decision on a construction dispute is binding absent fraud, gross mistake necessarily implying bad faith, or failure to exercise honest judgment, but a decision without a reasonable basis or patently erroneous is the legal equivalent of bad faith.

After-acquired evidence of employee misconduct serious enough that the employer would have fired for it does not bar all relief for a discriminatory discharge, but it generally forecloses reinstatement and front pay and makes the period from discharge to discovery the starting point for backpay.

A promise in a sale contract to pay the prevailing party's litigation costs is divisible from the sale and remains enforceable even though the sale itself became void when its financing condition failed.

A seller's tolerance of late payment does not oblige it to forbear indefinitely; absent an intentional relinquishment of the right to payment, it may insist on payment after giving notice and the cure period the contract provides.

A party to a contract outside the UCC may suspend performance when the other side ignores its reasonable requests for assurance, applying the principle of UCC section 2-609 as generalized in Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 251.

The cost of reinstating defective building work is recoverable only if the work is necessary to produce conformity and reasonable to undertake; where it is not, the owner may be awarded damages for loss of amenity rather than nothing.

Disgorgement of a breaching party's profits is available as restitution case by case, where the breach is conscious and substantial and damages are inadequate, but the profits must be apportioned between the parties' respective contributions.
A sale of a contracting corporation's stock is not an assignment of the corporation's contract or a delegation of its duties where the corporation continues to exist and perform as a separate entity.

Under former Civil Code article 1143, a creditor of a contractual obligation may demand destruction of what was done in breach of the commitment, and the absence of demonstrated prejudice does not justify refusing restoration.

Under CISG Article 74 a buyer recovers the foreseeable loss, including lost profit, caused by the seller's breach; lost profit is computed by deducting variable but not fixed costs, and actual expenditures wasted because of the breach are recoverable in addition without duplicating lost profits.

Under New York law, promissory estoppel requires a clear and unambiguous promise, reasonable and foreseeable reliance, and injury from that reliance, and it can support reliance damages, including properly attributable overhead, even though the parties never formed the contemplated contract.

The implied covenant of good faith requires a party to actually exercise discretion it has promised to exercise and to do so neither arbitrarily nor irrationally, but it cannot create obligations inconsistent with the contract's terms.

An offer to dedicate land to public use must be accepted by a manifest public act while the offer is still open; it ends by lapse after an unreasonable delay or by withdrawal through private use inconsistent with public ownership.

Because wrongful discharge under a just-cause employment agreement sounds in contract, the tort collateral-source rule does not apply, and unemployment compensation the employee received must be deducted from damages so that recovery does not exceed the position performance would have produced.

An employer asserting failure to mitigate bears the burden of proving both that substantially equivalent positions were available and that the employee failed to exercise reasonable diligence in seeking them.

A buyer need not cover by impractical or disproportionately expensive means or beyond its financial resources; reasonableness of cover is judged by good faith and the circumstances at the time, and the seller bears the burden of proving an unreasonable failure to avoid loss.

Seven Justices, without a single majority rationale, held that when the Government contractually assumes the risk of a change in regulatory law, it is liable in damages if later legislation prevents the promised performance, and the special sovereign defenses do not excuse it.

A contract price is due only upon performance, even if fixed as a lump sum, so once termination of the contract is recognized the other party recovers damages, absent a penalty clause, rather than the full agreed price.

Under promissory estoppel, a man who is neither a child's biological nor adoptive father may be bound to support the child where he knowingly promised to assume fatherhood and the mother and child relied to their detriment.

In testing a public contract against a constitutional ban on gifts of public funds, the court asks whether consideration is legally sufficient rather than comparing market values, absent a showing of donative intent or grossly inadequate return.

Under North Carolina law a contract can be accepted through a course of conduct without a signed writing, and a party who performs knowing the other side has consistently rejected a proposed term may be found to have accepted a counteroffer omitting it.

A pay-if-paid clause making the owner's payment a condition precedent to a general contractor's duty to pay a subcontractor is unenforceable as contrary to public policy, because it indirectly waives the subcontractor's protected mechanics' lien rights.

According to the 1997 Connecticut Appellate Court, a third party may enforce a contract as an intended beneficiary when the promisee's purpose was to fulfill its own obligation to that party; mere foreseeability is not enough.

A seller may propose a contract whose written terms arrive with the product and invite acceptance by retention; a buyer who keeps the product beyond the stated return period after an opportunity to read the terms accepts them, including an arbitration clause.

Mortgages and contracts require valid consideration, and formal documents cannot supply a bargained exchange the parties never intended; a circular gift-and-loan-back arrangement in which no control over funds is surrendered creates neither a valid gift nor an enforceable debt.

A buyer who keeps mail-order goods beyond the stated return period assents to the terms enclosed with them, but an arbitration term whose costs effectively leave consumers without an accessible forum can be unenforceable for substantive unconscionability alone.

A deed reservation of coal and other minerals unambiguously includes oil and gas, at least absent an allegation that exercising the mineral rights unduly affects the surface estate, and disagreement over a term's meaning does not alone make it ambiguous.

A lawyer employed by a law firm cannot bring a retaliatory-discharge tort claim against the firm for objecting to its unlawful practices, because the lawyer's own ethical obligations already adequately safeguard the public policy at stake.

Where a contract conditions a duty on approval by a party's own internal division, that party must consider approval in good faith but does not promise to approve, and may rely on the condition absent bad faith.

In an employee-handbook contract action, after-acquired evidence of misconduct is a complete defense only if the employer proves by clear and convincing evidence that the misconduct was severe enough that it would in fact have fired the employee on that ground alone.

After-acquired evidence of employee misconduct is a defense to a contract claim for discharge-related wages and benefits if the employer would have fired the employee for it, but in a wrongful-discharge tort action it limits remedies rather than barring liability.

A stipulated-damages clause is enforceable, not a penalty, when damages were difficult to ascertain at formation, the parties made a reasonable effort to estimate them, and the amount is reasonably related to probable damage; a court may not substitute its own measure.

Under New York law a third party is an intended beneficiary only if no one else can recover for the promisor's breach or the contract's language otherwise clearly shows intent to permit third-party enforcement; an anti-assignment clause alone does not defeat that status.

A third party may enforce a contract only if both contracting parties intended the promisor to assume a direct obligation to that third party; a foreseeable benefit, or intent merely to confer a benefit, is not enough.

An advertisement is ordinarily an invitation to make offers, not an offer, and whether a communication is an offer is judged by what an objective reasonable person would understand, so an evident joke creates no power of acceptance.

As this intermediate court reasoned before it was reversed, a dealer's advertisement of one identified car at a stated price, read with the advertised-price statute, is an offer accepted by tender, and a good-faith unilateral mistake does not necessarily erase it.

An oral offer made face to face ordinarily ends with the conversation unless a contrary intention appears; if the offeror invites a later answer and states no deadline, the offer remains open for a reasonable time determined by the circumstances.

A merchant seller's implied warranty of merchantability arises by operation of law from the seller-buyer relationship, and a usage of trade excludes it only if the parties share the trade or both knew or should have known of it.

An agreement fixing a spouse's economic rights on divorce, made mid-marriage under the other spouse's threat to divorce, arises in an inherently coercive setting and is enforced only if fair both when signed and when enforcement is sought.

A percentage-rent clause based on gross sales is read in the context of the whole lease, and does not reach government-owned receipts that merely pass through the tenant, though it does reach the compensation the tenant retains for handling them.

An employee noncompetition covenant is enforceable only to protect an employer interest beyond ordinary competition, such as specialized training, confidential information and customer relationships taken together, and a court may narrow an overbroad covenant and resolve its ambiguities in the employee's favor.

Under Mississippi precedent a proved oral agreement to devise real property does not support specific performance; the promisee who relied may recover money, here through a constructive trust for the amount invested plus interest.

A forum-selection clause in an online membership agreement binds a subscriber who had the opportunity to scroll through the terms and clicked to accept, where the clause was reasonably presented and not concealed.

The public-policy exception to at-will employment is narrow and requires a discharge for a reason that violates an important public policy; statutes on family leave and pregnancy do not create a policy requiring employers to grant flexible work schedules.
A contestant who agrees that the contest judges' decisions are final is bound by them absent fraud, gross mistake or lack of good faith.

A signed offer to purchase that fixes the material terms can be a binding contract, if the parties so intend, even though it contemplates a later formal agreement, and a deadline for executing that agreement is a condition that can be waived by conduct.

A cancellation schedule is enforceable as liquidated damages when, judged at formation, it reasonably estimates the probable loss from declining opportunities to rebook; once the clause is valid, the non-breaching party's actual efforts to rebook are irrelevant.

A liquidated-damages clause is judged from the circumstances at contract formation: it is enforceable if damages were then difficult to determine and the sum reasonably forecast expected damage, without a retrospective second look at actual loss.

An insurer's duty of good faith does not extend to everyone entitled to insurance money; a contractual or statutory relationship is required, and an injured person covered by a premises owner's liability policy is only an incidental beneficiary for purposes of a bad-faith claim.

A clause requiring consent to assignment limits the right but not the power to assign; an unauthorized assignment is effective, though a breach, unless the agreement clearly manifests that a nonconforming assignment is void or ineffective.

A seller's statement creates an express warranty only if it is an affirmation, promise or description relating to the goods actually sold that forms part of the basis of the bargain; statements about differently configured goods and general commendation do not.

Under the UCC, a trade usage may supply an exclusive limitation of remedies as part of the parties' agreement, and a limited remedy that includes return and refund does not fail of its essential purpose merely because repair attempts were unsuccessful.

Competition for an at-will client is generally privileged absent fraud or other unlawful means, and Illinois promissory fraud requires a scheme to defraud supported by more than the allegedly false promise alone.

Participating in a free promotional contest can be consideration for the promoter's promise of a prize when the participant's requested acts, such as visiting, waiting and supplying information, are what the promoter sought to induce.

When the Government repudiates or substantially breaches a contract, the other party may obtain restitution of the payments it made, even if the contract would not ultimately have been profitable, provided it has not waived that right.

A lowest responsible bidder wrongfully denied a public contract may recover its reasonable bid preparation costs from the public entity under promissory estoppel, but not the profits it expected to earn from performing the contract.

A mandatory employment arbitration agreement may cover FEHA claims only if it preserves the employee's unwaivable statutory rights, and an adhesive agreement is unconscionable if it requires arbitration of the employee's claims but not the employer's corresponding claims without a reasonable business justification.

A procedurally unconscionable employment arbitration agreement is still enforced where its only substantively unconscionable term can be deleted without adding obligations or undermining the agreement's central purpose.

The public-policy wrongful-discharge tort is available only when the employee otherwise has no remedy, so an existing statutory remedy for the retaliation precludes the common-law claim even if that remedy is less favorable than a private action.

A mortgage contingency carries an implied promise to use reasonable efforts to obtain financing, but the buyer need not make futile applications, so one application can suffice when the circumstances show others would not succeed.

A party adversely affected by a mutual mistake cannot rescind if it bore the risk of the mistake, as when it knew it had only limited knowledge of the relevant facts but treated that knowledge as sufficient.

A nonclient can enforce a lawyer's retainer as a third-party beneficiary only if the retainer was intended to benefit it and the benefit is immediate enough to show the contracting parties assumed a duty to compensate it; an indirect economic benefit is not enough.

Between merchants under UCC section 2-207(2), additional terms in an acceptance become part of the contract unless an exception applies, and the party opposing inclusion bears the burden of proving that the term materially alters the contract.

UCC section 2-207 applies even when only one written form is exchanged; where the buyer is the offeror and is not a merchant, terms enclosed with the goods are proposals for additional terms that bind the buyer only on express assent, not on mere retention.

A party may rescind for a good-faith unilateral mistake of fact the other party neither caused nor had reason to know of, if the mistake concerns a basic assumption, materially affects the exchange, the mistaken party does not bear the risk, and enforcement would be unconscionable.

When expressly conditional and inconsistent forms fail to form a written contract and the parties' conduct establishes one, section 2-207(3) alone determines its terms: those on which the writings agree plus supplementary terms supplied by other Code provisions.

Relief from a paternity judgment under Rule 60(b)(5) or (6) must be sought within a reasonable time, and conclusive genetic evidence of nonpaternity does not automatically undo legal paternity that a man voluntarily acknowledged and long left unchallenged.

Where contract language reasonably supports competing meanings the factfinder ordinarily resolves it; a reasonable-efforts duty is not implied into an exclusive license carrying a substantial guaranteed royalty, but the implied covenant of good faith can still be breached.

Arbitration terms are subject to ordinary contract defenses; place-and-manner terms that are procedurally and substantively unconscionable in their commercial setting may be severed, leaving the agreement to arbitrate enforceable, where unconscionability does not permeate the agreement.

A cardholder whose agreement authorizes amendment on notice is bound by a clearly noticed arbitration amendment he had a meaningful opportunity to reject and did not, unless he establishes a generally applicable contract defense to the arbitration agreement itself.

Under Florida's section 542.335, a third party may enforce a business restrictive covenant only if the covenant expressly identifies that person as a beneficiary and expressly states that it is for that person's benefit; a covenant in the claimant's own contract remains enforceable.

Under the Michigan wine-distribution statute, a supplier may not withhold consent to a distributor's business transfer where the proposed transferee meets the supplier's material and reasonable qualifications and standards, and whether it does can be a question of fact.

Under the binding force of agreements, a court that has found an express contractual commitment to construct, and a clause giving that contract priority over other documents, may not rely on subordinate documents to deny performance of the construction obligation.

Under UCC section 2-609 a party may demand adequate assurance only when reasonable grounds for insecurity exist; though insecurity and adequacy are ordinarily fact questions, summary judgment is proper where no reasonable jury could find the demand justified or the response inadequate.

Legal services can fall within the class of necessaries that overcomes an infancy defense, but whether particular services were actually necessary is a question of fact, and if they were the minor owes only their reasonable value.

Promissory fraud requires the ordinary fraud elements plus an intention, when the promise was made, not to perform and to deceive; nonperformance alone is insufficient, but later circumstances may supply circumstantial evidence of that earlier intent.

A difference in treatment is not discrimination under article 26 of the Covenant when it rests on objective and reasonable grounds, and a ban on dwarf tossing met that test as a measure protecting public order and human dignity.

Respect for human dignity is a component of public order, so a municipal authority may prohibit an attraction that infringes dignity even without particular local circumstances and even though the participant consents and is paid.

Under New York law, a clear, complete writing is enforced according to its terms, and silence about a particular use does not make an unconditional transfer of ownership ambiguous or reserve that use to the grantor.
An online user's click manifests assent to contract terms only when the interface reasonably alerts the user that terms exist and that the click signifies agreement to them.

A force majeure clause excusing performance made inadvisable by a listed event is construed objectively in light of its risk-allocation function, and economic undesirability following such an event does not by itself excuse performance.

A creditor of an unpaid contractual money obligation may choose payment of the price rather than damages or dissolution, and a court that has rejected every ground for undoing the contract may not substitute damages for the price.

An employee's salary is consideration for her promise to arbitrate without a matching employer promise, and section 2 of the FAA bars states from burdening arbitration clauses more than other terms in form contracts.
Under Mississippi law as the Fifth Circuit read it, illiteracy does not defeat a signed agreement; a signer who cannot read must obtain assistance, and the other party need not explain the document.

Those who benefit from a government contract are presumed incidental beneficiaries and may enforce it only if the contract's precise language shows a clear intent to give them enforceable rights; explicit mention of their class is not by itself sufficient.
An innocent misrepresentation, made without any indication that the speaker knew it was inaccurate, can justify rescission of a transaction it induced.

The Contract Disputes Act governs only claims between the United States and its contractors, so it does not strip a district court of jurisdiction over an alleged third-party beneficiary's suit against a private supplier under a federal procurement contract.

Under New York law, a party that merely benefits commercially from another's contract cannot sue on it as an intended beneficiary where the promisee itself can enforce the promise and the agreement shows no intention to give the third party its own enforcement right.

Under former Civil Code article 1184, a party whose counterparty has not performed may compel performance when it is possible, so a proven departure from contractual specifications cannot be left uncorrected merely because the building is usable and the term nonessential.

Under the implied warranty of merchantability, fitness for ordinary purposes is measured by the reasonable expectations of an ordinary user or purchaser, not by the subjective expectations of the particular person who used the product.

A corporation with an imputed racial identity may sue under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 for discrimination in contract performance, and a nominal-damages award does not show absence of injury, but a punitive award must satisfy constitutional limits of reprehensibility, relation to harm and comparable sanctions.

Under UCC § 9-404(a)(1), an assignee's rights are subject to all terms of the agreement between the account debtor and the assignor and to defenses arising from that transaction, regardless of when the account debtor received notice of the assignment.

Under New York General Business Law § 394-c as applied in 2005, a dating-service contract that does not promise a specified number of referrals per month may charge at most $25, and an injured consumer may recover actual damages or $50, whichever is greater.

Consideration is distinguished from a conditional gift by reciprocal inducement: the promise must induce the detriment and the detriment must induce the promise, and no actual negotiation over the terms is required.

A contract for the sale of goods still requires a bargain in fact; silence in response to an unsigned confirmation is not acceptance unless the parties' relationship or course of dealing justifies expecting a reply.

An advertisement is deceptive if a representation is likely to mislead reasonable consumers and is material; strong health claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence, and a placebo response does not substantiate a claim of inherent effectiveness.

Separately itemized prices do not by themselves make a contract divisible; whether a failure to supply one listed service is a material breach of an entire contract is a question of fact, and a funeral contract can support foreseeable emotional-distress damages.

Under California Uniform Commercial Code section 9403, an assignee taking for value, in good faith and without notice of claims or defenses may enforce an account debtor's waiver of defenses, despite nondelivery of the goods and a later rescission between the original parties.

An enforceable arbitration agreement requires a writing, an unambiguous intent to submit to arbitration, and bilateral consideration; a handbook arbitration clause acknowledged only as non-contractual information, and changeable by the employer at any time without notice, lacks assent and consideration.

Under the CISG, which has no parol evidence rule, a merger clause bars evidence of prior oral understandings only if both parties shared the intention to be bound by it, so negotiations must be considered under Article 8 even when they contradict the writing.

An offer to exchange a large bill for smaller bills is a proposed contract supported by consideration, even though the face values are equal and the business charges no fee and gains no immediate profit.

Under Texas law as applied by the Tenth Circuit, when an employee keeps working after a written contract of more than one year expires, an implied renewal on an indefinite or month-to-month basis is not barred by the one-year provision of the statute of frauds.

The suretyship provision of the statute of frauds applies to promises to answer for another's future as well as existing debt, but a suretyship promise made mainly to serve the promisor's own pecuniary or business interest falls outside the writing requirement.

A promissory-fraud claim survives a motion to dismiss when the plaintiff specifically alleges facts, beyond later nonperformance, showing the promisor had no intention to perform when the promise was made.

A buyer's precontract examination excludes the implied warranty of merchantability only for defects that the examination ought, in the circumstances, to have revealed, and the warranty survives compliance with buyer specifications that are consistent with it.

A contract obtained through bribery cannot sustain claims before a tribunal as a matter of public policy, and a contract procured by bribing the other party's agent is voidable at that principal's option until informed affirmation.

A disappointed bidder's claim that the government denied its proposal fair and honest consideration accrues when the bidder has notice of the alleged concealed manipulation, not merely when it learns it lost the award.

An attorney who cannot complete an indivisible representation because of his own disbarment may not recover contract fees or the market value of his services, but only restitution measured by the benefit conferred on the client, less what the client has already paid.

A lawyer retained to represent a client against an adverse party in litigation owes that party no ordinary negligence duty as an intended beneficiary of the retainer, and a promise to hold security as custodian creates duties only once the security is delivered.

A court-appointed guardian's responsibility for the ward does not end by informally delegating the work to an assistant, and a lawyer remains responsible for ensuring that delegated legal responsibilities are completed properly.

An oral promise to pay another's debt is enforceable despite the suretyship statute of frauds when, looking to the entire transaction, the promisor's main purpose was to obtain a benefit for itself; the original debtor need not be released.

A ward under a valid adjudication-based guardianship cannot incur contractual duties, and the guardianship order gives constructive public notice of incapacity, so a seller without actual knowledge can neither enforce the contract nor claim restitution.

A negotiated no-reliance clause, unlike an integration clause, can defeat a fraud claim by making reliance on contrary oral statements unreasonable as a matter of law where the signer was sophisticated and advised by counsel.

Fraudulent misrepresentation requires both actual reliance and reliance that is reasonable under the circumstances, and summary judgment is proper when the content and context of the statements mean no reasonable jury could find either.

A contract made by a contractor lacking a statutorily required license is null and void, and an agency's relaxed enforcement or the other party's knowledge does not validate it; the contractor may recover only its actual costs through unjust enrichment.

Employees who work under a city service contract are intended third-party beneficiaries of the contractor's express promise to the city to comply with its living wage ordinance and may sue the contractor for breach of that promise.

An intended beneficiary of a proposed contract may assert rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1981; a person is an intended beneficiary when both parties intended the promisor to assume a direct obligation to that person, and foreseeable benefit alone is insufficient.

Under New York law, a contractual disclaimer of reliance that specifically addresses the subject of the alleged misrepresentations defeats the reasonable-reliance element of fraudulent inducement, so a release containing it can be enforced on a motion to dismiss.

A contract expressly made to benefit an identifiable class of third persons may be enforced by a member of that class, and the State, by entering a contract, waives immunity to the extent a party or beneficiary sues to enforce its undertaking.

A third person may enforce a contract only if the contracting parties clearly manifested at formation an intent to benefit that person; for government contracts there is a presumption against private beneficiary rights unless plain contractual language indicates an intended private enforcement right.

A requirements contract is supported by consideration even if the buyer has no requirements at formation, because UCC § 2-306 obligates the buyer to order its actual good-faith requirements from the seller.

A pet's classification as personal property does not categorically foreclose specific performance of an agreement about its ownership and possession, because money damages may not compensate sincere affection for and attachment to a particular animal.

A unilateral contract becomes enforceable when the requested performance is rendered, so an employer's promise to at-will employees, even if illusory when made, binds once the employees complete the performance it asked for.

Section 230(c)(1) bars state-law claims that treat an interactive computer service as the publisher of another's content, but not a promissory-estoppel claim whose duty arises from the provider's own enforceable promise to remove that content.

On this court's reasoning, an ordinary eBay auction does not, without further forum ties, purposefully direct the seller's conduct toward the winning bidder's state, because the seller cannot choose the winner's identity or location.

A counteroffer rejects the original offer, but a mere inquiry whether the offeror would consider different terms does not, so the offeree may still accept the original offer after the inquiry is refused.

Whether an oral agreement can be performed within one year turns on the terms the parties actually agreed to, not on a party's ability to perform sooner; and a voice on a secret recording is not an electronic signature without intent to sign.

A party who could avoid an agreement for undue influence or duress loses that power by ratification, as by keeping the benefits and delaying unreasonably in disaffirming after the pressure has ceased.

Under the False Claims Act as then worded, a demand on a grantee or other recipient is a claim if the United States provided any portion of the money; and a staffing figure appearing only in a cost estimate is not a contractual commitment.

As the Appellate Division held before being reversed, a release of ordinary negligence cannot defeat personal-injury liability that the exceptions in New Jersey's equine-activities statute preserve, because those exceptions are part of the legislature's allocation of risk.

Specific performance of a contract to sell land requires clear and convincing proof of a valid contract, the claimant's readiness, willingness and ability to perform, and a balance of equities favoring enforcement, and the decree may add interest to compensate delayed payment.

Under Massachusetts law, which follows Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 302, the promisor and promisee may agree to exclude third-party enforcement, and an express exclusion defeats a claim of intended-beneficiary status.

Because wrongful-death claims under the Texas statute are entirely derivative of the decedent's rights, the statutory beneficiaries stand in the decedent's legal position and are bound by an arbitration agreement the decedent signed.

A communication is not an offer when the recipient knows or should know that further assent is contemplated, and a party who knows of the other side's obvious computational mistake cannot bind it by purporting to accept.

A term is implied in fact only where necessary, tested by business efficacy and the officious bystander together, and the court declined to imply a general duty of good faith in law; an entire-agreement clause excludes implied terms only by clear language.

Under New York law, a specific disclaimer of reliance on representations about the very subject of the alleged fraud ordinarily bars a fraudulent-inducement claim, and the peculiar-knowledge exception does not ordinarily protect someone who could have insisted on a written assurance.

Under Arizona's Gift Clause a public contractual expenditure needs a public purpose and consideration not so disproportionately low that the deal is a subsidy, and consideration counts only what the private party actually promised, not anticipated indirect public benefits.
A modification of a cooperation agreement requires objective mutual assent and new lawful consideration; promising testimony the defendant was already obligated to give supplies none.

Under New Jersey's Equine Activities Liability Act, exceptions to the bar on claims from inherent risks are strictly but reasonably construed: faulty equipment means equipment itself faulty, and negligent disregard requires a breach of a recognized operator duty that caused the injury.

Emotional-distress damages for breach of contract may be available when they are both foreseeable from breach and explicitly within the parties' contemplation at formation, judged by the agreement's nature and language and the parties' reasonable expectations.

Travelers for whom a group proposed to contract for lodging may assert rights as intended third-party beneficiaries under section 1981, and their common beneficiary position can support class certification under Rule 23(b)(3).

Part performance takes an oral land sale outside the statute of frauds when an outsider knowing the circumstances would naturally and reasonably infer a land contract; the performance need not be explicable only by the contract, and equity may supply fair market price and reasonable time.

A contract term is unconscionable and unenforceable when, judged at formation, an absence of meaningful choice combines with terms so one-sided that they oppress or unfairly surprise a party; the question is one of law for the court.

Assent to a contract modification is judged by objective manifestations, and a reply that varies the proposal is a counteroffer that the other party can accept by its response and immediate performance, including in an instant-message exchange.

Under Florida's UCC section 672.609, failure to give adequate assurance within a reasonable time after a justified written demand is a repudiation, and whether assurances were adequate is ordinarily a question of fact.

A seller's factual assurance about goods that forms the basis of the bargain is an express warranty under UCC 2-313, and emotional or spiritual injury and foreseeable consequential costs from its breach may be pursued under UCC 2-715.

Where a government form contract merely incorporates statutory obligations for which Congress provided no private right of action, the statute's intended recipients cannot enforce those same obligations by suing as third-party beneficiaries of the contract.

A nonsignatory is estopped from refusing arbitration only if it receives a direct benefit flowing from the agreement containing the arbitration clause, not merely from the relationship between its parties, or asserts claims that depend on that agreement's provisions.

Where a policy lets the insured reinstate lapsed coverage by payment alone, payment by an authorized mailed check is effective under the mailbox rule when the check is dispatched to the insurer, not when it is received or negotiated.

As a federal court predicted Massachusetts law, a lender's promise to consider a borrower for a loan modification that induces the borrower to default can support a promissory-estoppel claim despite indefinite modification terms, with relief aimed at restoring the position lost through reliance.

Under Texas law, a loan agreement over $50,000, including a financial institution's promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation, must be in a signed writing, and promissory estoppel avoids that requirement only if the promisor promised to sign a complying written document.

Part performance takes an oral land contract out of the statute of frauds only on clear and convincing proof of definite terms and acts exclusively referable to the contract; restitution for benefits conferred remains available, measured by the value to the recipient.

Unconscionability remains a generally applicable contract defense to an arbitration agreement after Concepcion, and a court may refuse to sever where multiple one-sided terms show arbitration was structured as an inferior forum favoring the stronger party.

The Airline Deregulation Act preempts a state-law implied covenant of good faith claim that relates to airline prices, routes or services when the covenant is a state-imposed obligation that enlarges the airline's voluntarily adopted contractual undertakings.

In enforcing a congressionally approved interstate compact under its equitable original jurisdiction, the Court may order partial disgorgement of a breaching State's gains where the State consciously disregarded the other State's known rights, to stabilize the compact and deter recurrence.

Where the purpose of a notice condition is undisputedly fulfilled by timely actual notice, a court may excuse strict compliance with the prescribed method of delivery to avoid disproportionate forfeiture, unless the condition was a material part of the agreed exchange.

A user who lacks actual notice of online terms is bound if a reasonably prudent user would be on inquiry notice of them through reasonably conspicuous notice and the user unambiguously manifests assent, even without clicking a button labeled I agree.

Under California law an arbitration agreement is unenforceable only if both procedurally and substantively unconscionable on a sliding scale, and a court may sever unconscionable terms that are collateral to the agreement's lawful central purpose and enforce the rest.

Under the Federal Arbitration Act, an ambiguous arbitration agreement cannot supply the contractual basis required to compel class arbitration, and the state-law rule construing ambiguity against the drafter cannot substitute for that basis.

Under Georgia law a non-party may enforce only those contract provisions that the agreement as a whole clearly shows were intended for that person's benefit; practical benefit from correct performance makes a person only an incidental beneficiary.

Under Ohio law impossibility is an affirmative defense requiring an unforeseen event after contracting that makes performance impossible without the promisor's fault; reasonably foreseeable difficulties and mere difficulty or burden do not excuse performance.
A tenant's loss of clients and inability to afford rent because of the pandemic neither frustrates the purpose of an office lease nor makes performance objectively impossible.

Frustration of purpose requires complete destruction of the basis of the contract; a tenant that can still use leased premises for part of its intended business shows only partial frustration, which does not excuse rent.

A force-majeure clause excusing performance hindered by governmental orders excuses a tenant's rent to the extent the order proximately caused its inability to generate revenue, so rent is reduced in proportion and not eliminated where some operations remain permitted.

Under New York's prevention doctrine a party may not avoid a contractual duty by frustrating the occurrence of a condition to it, and enforcing an airline's own promised remedies through that doctrine is not preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act.

On the casebook's account, increased difficulty or cost alone, such as a fall in anticipated revenue, does not establish impracticability excusing an enforceable payment obligation; additional conditions are required.

Where a lease's force majeure clause allocates the risk of a contingency and expressly preserves the duty to pay rent, common-law frustration, impossibility and failure of consideration do not supply discharge or abatement contrary to the agreed terms.
Read the full case account and its source limitations.

A contract claim against a college requires a specific, concrete promise, but unjust enrichment may be pleaded in the alternative while it remains unresolved whether an enforceable contract term governs retention of the money paid.
An online contract requires reasonable notice of the terms and a reasonable manifestation of assent to them, and the party seeking to enforce the contract bears the burden of showing both.

Under New York UCC §2-316(2) and §1-201(b)(10), a written disclaimer of implied warranties is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to notice it from its overall presentation, and the statute sets no absolute rule that it must appear before the signature.

Under the prevention doctrine, a party whose breach of contract materially contributes to the nonoccurrence of a condition cannot rely on that nonoccurrence, so a buyer who breaches its financing-efforts covenant cannot invoke the unfunded-debt condition to avoid specific performance.

When a prosecutor makes an unconditional decision not to prosecute for the purpose of inducing reliance, and the defendant reasonably relies on it to the detriment of the privilege against self-incrimination, due process and fundamental fairness require that the decision be enforced.

Under Sherman Act section 1, concerted action turns on economic substance: an agreement that joins independent decisionmakers pursuing distinct economic interests on the challenged decision, here franchise restaurants' hiring, is concerted action despite a common enterprise.

The temporary restraining order states no general rule; it shows only that a court granted interim relief directing a hiring hospital either to lend staff to, or to stop hiring from, the employer whose team was leaving.

Under New York's price-gouging statute, a prima facie case of an unconscionably excessive price may be shown by comparing the challenged price with the seller's usual pre-disruption price; a single violation suffices, and the seller may rebut by proving added costs.
A court may stay litigation over a merger agreement for a defined period to let the parties close, while fixing a deadline after which the case returns promptly to trial if closing fails.

A recipient of federal funds under Spending Clause antidiscrimination statutes is on notice only of remedies traditionally available for breach of contract, and emotional-distress damages, generally unavailable in contract, are therefore not recoverable in the implied private action.

Emotional-distress damages for breach of contract require both that emotional injury be foreseeable and that the contract's specific language and obligations show the parties explicitly contemplated such damages at formation; foreseeability alone is not enough.

Where a lease's force majeure clause relieves a party from liability when a specified event prevents performance and contains no proviso preserving rent, the rent obligation is excused during the event rather than merely delayed.

Under Wyoming law, third-party-beneficiary intent is determined from the agreement as a whole and the circumstances of its execution, so an unambiguous clause disclaiming third-party rights is evidence of intent but does not alone resolve beneficiary status.

Under California law, economic duress requires a wrongful act coercive enough to induce a reasonably prudent person lacking a reasonable alternative to agree, and undue influence requires undue susceptibility and excessive pressure overbearing the will; the party seeking rescission bears the burden.

A noncompetition covenant is prima facie invalid and the employer must prove it reasonable; a court will not rewrite an unreasonable covenant into a reasonable one, so a covenant with unreasonable duration or geography is void.

Impracticability excuses performance only when a supervening extreme event actually causes the inability to perform the promised obligation and the risk was not assigned to the promisor; frustration requires destruction of a principal purpose shared by both parties.

Government closure orders that bar a tenant's business but do not prevent the payment of rent do not excuse rent under force majeure or impossibility, and a temporary closure does not frustrate a long-term lease whose value is not destroyed.

A preliminary injunction requires both a likelihood of success and likely immediate, irreparable injury; ordinary unrecoverable compliance costs and speculative employee departures are not irreparable harm.

Under the major questions doctrine, an agency's extraordinary assertion of economic and political power needs clear congressional authorization, which the general rulemaking language of FTC Act sections 5 and 6(g) likely did not supply for a near-total noncompete ban.

Section 6(g) of the FTC Act is a housekeeping provision that does not authorize substantive legislative rules on unfair methods of competition, and a categorical nationwide noncompete ban lacking a reasoned explanation is arbitrary and capricious and must be set aside.

Under Swiss Code of Obligations articles 161 and 163, a contractual penalty is forfeited without proof of damage, but a court reduces it in its discretion when it is grossly disproportionate to the creditor's interest in full enforcement at the breach.
The translated excerpt upholds reduction of a contractual penalty to CHF 10,000 for a minor breach with no demonstrated damage or risk, while preserving a punitive function for the clause.

Under ordinary state contract-formation principles, an online amendment adding an arbitration clause binds existing users only with actual or constructive notice, and a unilateral modification clause silent about accrued claims does not reach claims that accrued before the amendment.

steps.note: Chancery may grant relief in equity and conscience after a judgment valid at common law, because equity acts on the party's conscience and does not reverse the legal judgment on the point adjudicated.

On a demurrer the court examines the whole pleading record for an earlier substantive defect, so a plaintiff does not automatically win because the defendant's last pleading is bad if the plaintiff's own earlier pleading fails to show a valid claim.

Facts showing that the defendant was only an involuntary instrument of the contact deny the battery and belong under the general issue; they cannot be pleaded as a justification, which must confess the battery and then avoid it.

A plaintiff who has recovered damages for a battery cannot bring a further action for later physical consequences of the same battery; the first recovery compensates the whole damage and bars the second suit.
A person whose goods have been wrongfully sold may waive the tort, treat the sale as made with his consent, and recover the proceeds in indebitatus assumpsit as money had and received to his use.
A person who moves goods that obstruct access to his own property, as he has a right to do, does not commit a conversion merely by failing to put them back, even if the goods are later lost.

The action for money had and received lies wherever the defendant has received money that natural justice obliges him to refund, the law implying a debt as though upon a contract even without any actual agreement to repay.
Trover requires an injurious conversion; a wharfinger's bare failure to return goods that were lost or stolen from him is not evidence of conversion, and the proper remedy is an action on the case.

Trespass lies for a direct or immediate injury and case for a consequential one, and a defendant who throws a lighted squib into a crowd is answerable in trespass although others, acting under necessity to protect themselves, threw it on.

Under the forms of action, an injury produced by the immediate act complained of had to be pleaded in trespass and a merely consequential injury in case; calling the act negligent did not make case the proper form.

An action on the case, not trespass, was the proper form against a master for his servant's negligent collision, the court finding it difficult to regard a master as a trespasser for a servant's act not done at his command.

To maintain trover a plaintiff must have both a right of property and a right of possession, so an owner who has leased goods for a term that is still running cannot sue in trover for their wrongful taking.

An action on the case will lie for a collision charged to the defendants' negligent management, where the record does not show that the defendants themselves committed the immediately injurious act; after verdict the court presumes that negligence, not willfulness, was proved.
Trespass lies where the injury is the immediate result of force personally applied by the defendant, even if the defendant acted negligently rather than willfully.
A plaintiff may obtain reversal of a judgment when the record fails to establish the federal court's jurisdiction, even though the plaintiff chose that court.
Under the statutory diversity grant, where an interest is joint, every person representing that interest must be competent to sue, or liable to be sued, in the federal courts.

An action for trespass to land is a local action that can be brought only where the land lies, and a court does not acquire jurisdiction over it merely because the defendant resides or can be found in its district.

Congress may give federal courts original jurisdiction over any case in which a question of federal law forms an ingredient of the original cause, even though the case also involves other questions of fact or law.

The Bank of the United States could sue in federal Circuit Court under its charter regardless of the parties' citizenship, and a State's ownership interest in a defendant corporation does not make the suit one against the State.

Where an injury is caused by the defendant's carelessness and negligence, the plaintiff may sue in case even though the defendant's own immediate act produced the harm, provided the act was not willful.

As the Court then read the Rules of Decision Act, state judicial decisions on questions of general commercial law deserve respect but do not bind federal courts, which decide such questions by their own judgment; Erie later repudiated this doctrine.

Under the Kansas code, causes of action arising from the same transaction may be joined in one petition even though they fall in different categories, such as injury to the person and injury to character.

Under code pleading, a plaintiff who pleads and proves facts establishing a contract claim may recover although the complaint also alleges conversion; the surplus tort allegation is disregarded when defendants knew the operative facts and claim no surprise.

A final judgment on the merits bars a later action on the same claim as to every ground that was or could have been raised, but in an action on a different claim it is conclusive only of matters actually litigated and determined.

A party invoking a prior judgment as an estoppel must show, from the record or consistent extrinsic evidence, the precise question necessarily decided; if the judgment could rest on any of several distinct matters and the uncertainty is not removed, it is not conclusive of any one.

An ordinary personal money judgment against an absent nonresident requires personal service within the state or voluntary appearance; a state may reach a nonresident's local property only if it is brought under the court's control before judgment.

A judgment conclusively settles the demand adjudicated, but in a later suit on a different demand it binds only on points actually litigated and determined, not on a fact admitted merely by a pleading omission.

A federal judgment entered in a case where jurisdiction was erroneously exercised is not a nullity; it binds the parties and bars collateral attack in a later suit until it is reversed or otherwise judicially set aside.

A supplemental instruction may urge jurors in the minority to reconsider their views in light of the majority's, so long as it preserves the requirement that the verdict reflect each juror's own judgment rather than mere submission to others.

Due process requires that notice to a nonresident allow a reasonable time both to reach the court and to prepare a defense; a judgment entered on notice that is unreasonably short in the circumstances does not bind the defendant.

The mere fact that Congress authorized an action, such as an adverse suit to determine the right of possession of a mining claim, does not confer federal-question jurisdiction; jurisdiction requires a genuine federal question or another independent basis under the ordinary rules.

Where local law permits garnishment, personal service on a garnishee found within the state, even temporarily, gives its courts power to condemn the debt he owes, provided the garnishee's own creditor could have sued him there.

Under the theory-of-the-pleading approach, a complaint is judged by the cause of action it was designed to state, and a count framed as conversion that omits an element of conversion cannot be saved by treating it as one in contract.

For statutory federal-question jurisdiction, the plaintiff's statement of his own cause of action must establish the federal basis; anticipating a federal defense, and pleading a federal answer to it, does not make the suit arise under federal law.

Under the Seventh Amendment's Reexamination Clause as read in 1913, an appellate court that finds the evidence insufficient may not enter judgment against an unconditional general jury verdict but must order a new trial.

Absent fraud or collusion by the party seeking judgment, a state court may rely on a sheriff's facially regular return of service, and leaving the unserved defendant to a remedy against the sheriff on his bond does not deny due process.

A suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action, so a state-law claim for injury to business does not arise under the patent laws merely because a defense may require deciding patent validity or infringement.

Waiving a tort and suing on an implied promise may avoid the shorter tort limitation period, but it does not make an amendment adding new defendants relate back, and it cannot create liability in a successor state agency that has no authority to be sued.

A state may apply property within its borders, including a bank deposit owed to a nonresident, to an obligation such as alimony if the property is within the state, seized at the commencement of proceedings, and the owner has an opportunity to be heard.
