steps.note: Courts may enforce a specific legal duty on which individual rights depend but cannot direct an executive officer's political discretion, and when a statute conflicts with the Constitution a court deciding the case must give effect to the Constitution.

When Congress has prescribed the manner in which a law is to be executed, executive instructions that go beyond the statute cannot legalize an act the statute does not authorize or protect the officer who obeys them from liability in damages.

Congress may exercise its legislative discretion to revive an earlier law either expressly or conditionally, making its operation depend on a future event that the President is to declare by proclamation.

When Congress imposes on an executive officer a specific ministerial duty leaving no discretion, the officer is bound by law to perform it, a court with jurisdiction may compel it by mandamus, and the President's duty to execute the laws implies no power to dispense with them.

Absent a constitutional or statutory provision fixing an inferior officer's tenure, the power to remove that officer is incident to the power to appoint, so the officer serves at the discretion of the appointing authority.
Mandamus lies to compel an executive officer to perform a ministerial act, but not to direct how a department head exercises judgment in interpreting and administering a statute.

Summary executive collection of a balance due from a revenue officer, through a Treasury distress warrant issued without a prior judicial trial, is neither an exercise of Article III judicial power nor a denial of Fifth Amendment due process.

When a state imposes a tax or assessment on property and provides a way to contest it in the ordinary courts, with notice and a hearing appropriate to the case, the resulting judgment does not deprive the owner of property without due process of law.

When Congress vests the appointment of inferior officers in the head of a department, its power to choose that appointing mechanism carries the power to limit, restrict and regulate the removal of those officers.

A beneficiary who intentionally murders the testator to prevent revocation and obtain the estate may not take under the will or by intestate succession; statutes are construed in light of their purpose and the maxim that no one may profit from his own crime.

A federal officer held by a State for an act done in performing a duty under federal law, including a duty inferred from the Constitution or a marshal's general statutory responsibilities, may be discharged on federal habeas if he did no more than was necessary and proper.

A transaction within the letter of a statute may fall outside the statute where the legislation as a whole, the surrounding circumstances and the consequences show that the legislature did not intend to include it.

Congress does not delegate legislative power when it sets a contingency and its legal consequence and leaves the President to find and proclaim the contingency, any discretion over duration being execution of the law; and a duly authenticated enrolled act cannot be impeached by legislative journals.

Congress may enlarge the powers and duties of an existing office with duties germane to it without requiring the incumbent, already appointed through the constitutional process, to be nominated, confirmed and appointed again.

The national government may ask a court of equity to enjoin forcible obstruction of interstate commerce and the mails, even without a financial stake, and the court may punish disobedience of that injunction by contempt without a jury.

Authority to prescribe future rates is a legislative power of major importance that an agency holds only if Congress grants it in clear statutory language; a duty to enforce a reasonable-rate requirement does not imply it.

When a subordinate body decides whether a tax will be levied, its amount, and its allocation among particular taxpayers, each affected owner must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard, with argument and proof, before the assessment becomes irrevocably fixed.

Once Congress has legislated and indicated its will, it may authorize an administrator to fill in the details within the defined statutory field, and violation of such regulations may be punished as a crime when Congress itself makes the violation an offense and fixes the penalty.

Due process does not require an individual hearing before a general determination that applies to a community on a common basis; a hearing is required where a relatively small number of persons are exceptionally affected on individual grounds.

A long-continued executive practice, known to Congress and acquiesced in by it, raises a presumption of congressional consent that can authorize the President to withdraw public lands from private acquisition, although executive practice alone cannot create power.

A citizen's general interest in lawful administration of government and in avoiding wasted public money does not present an Article III case and does not entitle him to a judicial ruling on a constitutional amendment's validity.

A federal taxpayer's interest in the national treasury is too small, remote and indeterminable to support a suit to enjoin a federal expenditure; a litigant must show a direct injury suffered or immediately threatened by the statute's enforcement.

The power to remove executive officers appointed by the President with Senate consent is constitutionally vested in the President, and Congress may not make its exercise depend on the Senate's consent.
Congress may authorize an official or body to carry out its legislative policy so long as it lays down an intelligible principle to which that official or body must conform.

General statutory words are read in light of the purpose and conditions of their enactment, so a statute making persons qualified to vote liable for jury service did not reach women when women later gained the vote.

A general residual term in a criminal statute takes its meaning from ordinary usage and the specific list it follows, and a criminal law must give fair warning in language ordinary people understand; a motor vehicle statute so read does not reach aircraft.

Courts ordinarily give great weight to an executive department's construction of a statute it administers, but they are not bound by it, and a construction lacking uniformity and consistency has only the force of its valid reasons.

When an agency, exercising delegated legislative power, prescribes a reasonable rate for the future, it may not later, acting judicially, award reparations for charges that conformed to that rate while its order was in force.

Congress may not hand the President the legislative choice whether to prohibit conduct without declaring a policy, setting a standard, or specifying the circumstances and findings on which he is to act.

Congress may fix the terms of members of a body performing quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions and limit their removal by the President to specified causes; the President's unrestricted removal power recognized in Myers extends only to purely executive officers.

Congress may set policies and standards and leave subordinate rules and fact-finding to administrators, but it may not transfer its essential legislative function by giving the President substantially unrestricted authority to make binding codes for trades and industries.

A private individual who invokes judicial power to test the validity of legislative or executive action must show a direct injury sustained or immediately threatened; a general interest common to the public is not enough.

State senators whose votes would have defeated a ratification resolution have standing to claim those votes were overridden and rendered ineffective, but the effect of a state's prior rejection and of lapse of time on ratifying a constitutional amendment are political questions for Congress.

Where Congress entrusts an agency with applying a statutory term such as producer to particular arrangements, a reviewing court leaves the agency's classification undisturbed if it follows a fair hearing and is a just and reasoned application of the statute.
Under the review statute then in force, a Tax Court determination supported by the record and a reasonable legal basis must stand unless the reviewing court can identify a clear mistake of law.

A reviewing court must judge an administrative order on the grounds the agency actually relied upon, and it cannot uphold the order by supplying a policy judgment entrusted to the agency that the agency did not itself make.

Where a broad statutory term such as employee must be applied in the first instance by the agency administering the Act, the agency's determination is accepted if it has warrant in the record and a reasonable basis in law.

An agency's rulings, interpretations and opinions do not control the courts but carry persuasive weight that depends on the care of their consideration, the soundness of their reasoning, their consistency with earlier and later positions, and other circumstances making them persuasive.

A delegation is valid when Congress states the policy, chooses the means and sets standards definite enough for a court to tell whether its will was obeyed, and Congress may confine challenges to a regulation's validity to an exclusive, adequate review route.

When two bona fide broadcast applications under the Communications Act are mutually exclusive, the Commission may not grant one without hearing both, because the grant substantially nullifies the other applicant's statutory opportunity to be heard.

After a remand an agency may reach the same result on a newly stated, statutorily authorized rationale, and the choice between making policy by general rule or by individual adjudication lies primarily within the agency's informed discretion.

In the D.C. Circuit majority's historical view, government employment is not life, liberty or property under the Fifth Amendment, so removal is not governed by due process, but an individualized bar on future federal employment is punishment requiring criminal-adjudication safeguards.

On whole-record review, a hearing examiner's findings resting on witness credibility must be given weight, and, as Learned Hand applied the remand, the Board may override them only on a very substantial preponderance in the recorded testimony.

Substantial evidence must be assessed on the whole record, including evidence that fairly detracts from the agency's conclusion and the examiner's report, which the Board may reject but which must be given the significance it reasonably deserves.

Presidential authority to act must come from Congress or the Constitution, and neither the Commander in Chief power nor the Take Care duty authorizes the President to seize private businesses to avert a strike without statutory authorization.

When Congress creates a body to adjudicate claims on evidence and law free from executive influence, the President has no power under the Constitution or the statute's silence to remove a member merely to install someone of his own choosing.

Absent explicit authorization from Congress or the President, executive officials may not deprive a person of private employment through a security-clearance proceeding that denies the traditional safeguards of confrontation and cross-examination.

Due process does not invariably require a trial-type hearing; the procedure due depends on the precise government function and the private interest affected, so a military commander with explicit authority may, on a rational stated security ground, withdraw a contractor employee's access without specific charges or a hearing.

A district court cannot compel NLRB officials to prosecute unfair-labor-practice charges, because Congress gave the General Counsel final authority over complaints; possible serious and irreparable harm does not supply jurisdiction absent the prescribed statutory route.

Where a statute requires rulemaking on the record under the APA, statistical summaries may be admitted, but opposing parties must have adequate access to the underlying material to test them; an agency that withholds it risks failing the substantial-evidence requirement.

Responsible representatives of the listening public may have standing to intervene in a broadcast license-renewal proceeding, although the Commission keeps broad discretion to regulate such participation, and a hearing is required when the Commission cannot make the statutory public-interest finding.

A court may overturn the FTC's refusal to postpone enforcement of a cease-and-desist order only for a patent abuse of discretion, asking whether the Commission's evaluation was patently arbitrary and capricious rather than weighing the evidence anew.

In informal rulemaking, the concise general statement of basis and purpose need not address every submission, but it must let a reviewing court see the major policy issues and why the agency resolved them as it did.

A specific agency order directed to a party in an adjudication is enforceable even though it rests on a general prospective requirement announced in an earlier adjudication without APA rulemaking, though no majority agreed on whether that earlier requirement was validly adopted.

A court cannot order the NLRB General Counsel to issue a complaint, but it may correct an erroneous legal construction that prevented any consideration of charges; the six-month limitations period does not begin before affected employees exist.

As the D.C. Circuit held before its judgment was vacated as moot, an SEC no-action position that the full Commission itself reviewed and approved is a reviewable order, and prosecutorial discretion does not shield an erroneous legal premise from review.

A reviewing court intervenes when an agency has not taken a hard look at the problem or engaged in reasoned decisionmaking, but once the agency has done so the court restrains itself even if it would have reached different findings or standards.

A plaintiff may seek review of agency action if it alleges injury in fact, economic or otherwise, and the interest it seeks to protect is arguably within the zone of interests protected or regulated by the statute invoked; no established legal interest is required.

Due process requires that a welfare recipient whose eligibility is disputed receive timely notice and an evidentiary hearing, with oral presentation and confrontation of adverse witnesses before an impartial decisionmaker, before benefits are terminated.

NLRA § 10(l) imposes a qualified mandatory duty: once a Regional Director finds reasonable cause and cannot secure cessation of the unlawful conduct, he must petition for temporary relief and issue a complaint unless the matter is too insubstantial.

The APA § 701(a)(2) exception for action committed to agency discretion is narrow and does not apply where statutes supply standards a court can apply; such action is reviewed on the full administrative record, not on litigation affidavits.

A written report by a physician who examined a disability claimant may be received and may constitute substantial evidence supporting an adverse finding, despite its hearsay character and contrary live testimony, when the claimant has not used the available right to subpoena the physician.

A broad delegation is constitutional when Congress determines the basic policy and the statute's text, purpose, history, duration and implied constraints supply standards by which Congress, courts and the public can assess compliance; breadth alone does not make it invalid.

An organization seeking APA review must show that it or its members are among those injured by the challenged action; aesthetic, environmental or recreational harm counts as injury in fact, but a longstanding interest in conservation does not itself establish injury.

Government may not deny a benefit on a basis that infringes protected speech even where no entitlement exists, and a property interest in continued employment may rest on rules or mutually explicit understandings, not only formal tenure, though a subjective expectation is insufficient.

Procedural due process applies only to deprivations of protected liberty or property, and a property interest requires a legitimate claim of entitlement grounded in independent rules or understandings such as state law, not a need, desire, or unilateral expectation.

As this district court held before being reversed, a Secretary who rejects a parkland highway route under § 4(f) must affirmatively find that a feasible and prudent alternative exists and designate it so that the decision can be reviewed.

APA sections 556 and 557 govern rulemaking only when a statute requires rules to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing or uses equivalent language; a statutory authority to act "after hearing" does not, and written submissions can satisfy it.

The Natural Gas Act gives the Federal Power Commission no jurisdiction over liquid petroleum, and rates subject to the Act's substantial-evidence review need a record whose factual premises parties could meaningfully test, though full formal APA procedures are not required.

A general statutory grant of power to make rules and regulations to carry out an act can authorize substantive rules defining the statutory standard, where later enforcement still proceeds through the adjudicatory procedures the statute requires.

In formal rulemaking, an agency may control repetitive questioning but may not wholly deny cross-examination necessary for full and true disclosure; and broad authority to set food identity standards still requires a meaningful exceptions procedure and adequately supported restrictions.

Section 4(f) prohibits approving a highway through parkland unless no feasible and prudent alternative exists, but it does not require the Secretary to identify a particular alternative route when he refuses approval.

An SEC staff no-action response that the Commission declines to review is not a Commission order reviewable under Exchange Act § 25(a), and a court cannot override the Commission's discretionary refusal to take up the matter.

As the Third Circuit held, the Secretary of Labor's refusal to sue to set aside a union election under the LMRDA is subject to narrow arbitrary-and-capricious review, and the Secretary must give an adequate statement of reasons for refusing.

The FTC's choice of pre-complaint consent-negotiation procedure, and its grant or denial of intervention in those negotiations, belong to agency enforcement discretion and are exempt from judicial review under APA § 701(a)(2).

A taxpayer lacks standing unless he challenges an exercise of the congressional taxing and spending power under a specific constitutional limit on that power, and an injury shared in common with the public is a generalized grievance.

Article III standing requires a concrete personal injury; a citizen's undifferentiated interest in constitutional government is an abstract injury, and neither the provision's supposed precision nor the absence of another plaintiff creates standing.

An agency's discretionary safety requirement is arbitrary under APA § 706(2)(A) when the agency does not adequately connect it to safety or support its practicability against concrete record objections, but a court may not reweigh requirements Congress expressly imposed.

A general statement of policy only announces what an agency intends to pursue and is exempt from notice and comment; unlike a substantive rule it is not a binding norm, so the agency must support the policy afresh whenever it applies it.

A nonprobationary federal employee removable only for cause may be discharged without a prior trial-type hearing where notice, a chance to respond and a full post-removal hearing are provided; no majority held that Congress may define the process along with the benefit.

The NLRA excludes all employees properly classified as managerial, and the Board may announce new principles through adjudication rather than rulemaking, a choice within its discretion unless it amounts to an abuse of discretion or violates the statute.

An agency may issue binding substantive regulations under a general rulemaking grant through notice and comment, reviewed under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard on the administrative record, but it must supply an explanation adequate for that review.

Under ejusdem generis, general words that follow specifically named things reach only things of the same kind, so other dangerous weapon after dagger, dirk and stiletto covers stabbing weapons and not a rifle.

The Secretary of Labor's decision not to sue to set aside a union election under Title IV of the LMRDA is reviewable under the APA, but review is ordinarily confined to whether the Secretary's statement of reasons shows an irrational, arbitrary, or capricious decision.

A court construes a statute's coverage independently, rather than deferring to any rational agency answer, where the agency adjudicates disputes rather than making policy, lacks a developed record and experience, and the question turns on legislative history and prior judicial decisions.

A court may consult legislative history even when statutory words appear clear on first examination; so read, the water statute's reference to radioactive materials excludes source, byproduct and special nuclear materials regulated under the Atomic Energy Act.

What procedural safeguards due process requires depends on the private interest affected, the risk of error under existing procedures and the probable value of additional or substitute safeguards, and the governmental interest, including fiscal and administrative burdens.

An appointee who exercises significant authority under federal law is an officer who must be appointed as the Appointments Clause prescribes; Congress and its presiding officers are not permissible appointing authorities for such officers.

The Eighth Amendment does not apply to disciplinary corporal punishment in public schools, and although such punishment implicates a protected liberty interest, a State's common-law limits and civil and criminal remedies provide due process without prior notice and a hearing.

A statute requiring a public hearing in an agency adjudication of disputed facts can trigger the APA's formal procedures under sections 554, 556, and 557 even without the words 'on the record,' and the agency may not rely on undisclosed material outside that record.

An agency using informal rulemaking must disclose the scientific material underlying its proposal so interested parties can comment meaningfully, and its statement of basis and purpose must answer the major objections that strike at the rule's central justification.

An agency may not dispense with notice and comment under the good-cause exception merely by characterizing its revised rules as compliance with new legislation, when the legislation leaves it new regulatory judgments to make.

Where state law permits a municipal utility to terminate service only for cause, the customer has a protected property interest, and due process requires notice explaining how to dispute a bill and a timely opportunity to present the complaint to an employee authorized to correct errors.

For informal rulemaking, APA section 553 generally sets the procedures courts may require, and a reviewing court ordinarily may not impose additional procedures beyond those required by the Constitution, the APA, and other governing statutes.

Under the plurality's reading of the Occupational Safety and Health Act, before adopting a permanent standard the Secretary must find that existing conditions pose a significant risk of material health impairment that the new standard can eliminate or lessen.

Under OSH Act § 6(b)(5), OSHA must set the standard for toxic materials that most adequately protects worker health to the extent feasible, meaning capable of being done, and the Act does not call for a separate comparison of costs and benefits.

Under a technology-forcing statute, an agency may set standards based on a prediction about technology not yet available if it answers theoretical objections, identifies the major steps still needed, and gives plausible reasons each can be completed in the available lead time.

Where settling claims is a necessary incident to resolving a major foreign-policy dispute and Congress has acquiesced in that kind of executive action, the President may suspend claims pending in American courts, though he has no plenary power to settle claims.

Under the D.C. Circuit's precedents, a plantwide bubble definition of stationary source was permissible for programs that preserve existing air quality but not for programs meant to improve air quality, so EPA could not use it in the nonattainment program.

A tester given racially discriminatory false information about housing availability suffers injury to a statutory right and has standing even without intent to rent, and an organization has standing when a defendant's practices perceptibly impair its services and drain its resources.
When the controversy underlying an appeal becomes moot, the appellate court vacates the judgment below and remands with instructions to dismiss the suit as moot, without deciding the merits.

As the casebook presents it, a commission's statutory placement in the executive branch did not foreclose arguments for its independence or prevent a preliminary injunction against presidential removal of its members.

An agency rescinding a rule is subject to ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious review and must examine the relevant material and explain the connection between its findings and its decision, including why it is abandoning its prior position.

When Congress takes action that is legislative in purpose and effect, altering the legal rights, duties, and relations of persons outside the Legislative Branch, it must comply with bicameral passage and presentment to the President unless the Constitution itself authorizes a different procedure.

An agency's refusal to invoke a permissive, nonexclusive enforcement power is committed to agency discretion under the APA, and § 1818(i)(1) of the banking statute bars a court from compelling the FDIC to issue what amounts to a cease-and-desist order.

The Federal Tort Claims Act's exception for claims arising in respect of the detention of goods by customs officers covers claims for negligent handling or storage of detained goods, not only harms caused by the detention itself.

Under the historical Chevron framework, a court asks first whether Congress has directly answered the precise question and, if it has not, whether the administering agency's answer is a permissible construction of the statute.

When a court reviews the factual support for agency action, the ordinary APA substantial-evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious standards require the same quantum of support; the distinctive role of the substantial-evidence provision is to require that support within the closed record of formal proceedings.

An agency's decision not to take enforcement action is presumptively unreviewable under APA § 701(a)(2), unless Congress has displaced the presumption by providing substantive guidelines that restrict the agency's enforcement discretion.

State law creates the property interest in continued public employment, but federal due process governs how it may be taken: a tenured public employee is entitled before termination to notice of the charges, an explanation of the employer's evidence, and an opportunity to respond.

An association may sue for its members when some members would have standing individually, the interests it seeks to protect are germane to its purpose, and neither the claim nor the relief requested requires individual members to participate.

Under Abbott Laboratories, a challenge to a contingent future agency action that may never occur is unripe absent immediate, direct and significant hardship, while an agency's immediately operative choices are reviewable and may be upheld under arbitrary-and-capricious review if the agency's path is reasonably discernible.

On substantial-evidence review, an agency may rest a health standard on cumulative, imperfect scientific evidence and scientifically supported conservative assumptions, but it must explain with evidence why a feasible further protection is unnecessary when significant risk remains.
Congress may not reserve to itself the power to remove, other than by impeachment, an officer charged with executing the laws, because removal power gives it practical control over execution.

An agency that adopts a new statutory interpretation in adjudication may ordinarily apply it in the case before it unless that would cause manifest injustice, assessed under the five Retail, Wholesale factors.

As the D.C. Circuit held in an opinion later vacated as moot, Heckler v. Chaney does not bar review of a decision to postpone a needed rule, and an agency may not rest that decision on considerations the statute does not permit.

For a plaintiff not itself regulated, the APA zone-of-interests test denies review only if the plaintiff's interests are so marginally related to or inconsistent with the statute's purposes that Congress cannot reasonably be assumed to have intended to permit the suit.

Absent explicit statutory or contractual authorization, a federal court taxing a prevailing party's expert witness fees as costs is bound by the limits of 28 U.S.C. §§ 1920 and 1821; Rule 54(d) gives no power to exceed them.

An agency's refusal to institute rulemaking is reviewable under a highly deferential standard, but the agency must consider the relevant factors, articulate the factual and policy bases of its decision, and have some record support for its factual assumptions.

An agency pronouncement that has present binding effect and does not genuinely leave the agency free to exercise discretion is a legislative rule requiring notice and comment, whatever label the agency gives it.

Conflicting interests among an association's members do not by themselves defeat associational standing, but the association may sue only if the members it represents themselves have standing, including a traceable and redressable injury.

Before a preliminary order temporarily reinstating a discharged whistleblower, due process requires that the employer receive notice of the allegations and the substance of the supporting evidence and a chance to respond, but not a prior evidentiary hearing with confrontation and cross-examination.

The D.C. Circuit panel held, before being reversed in Morrison v. Olson, that an independent counsel who is not subordinate to the Attorney General is a principal officer who cannot be appointed by a court, and that the statute impermissibly impaired executive control of prosecution.

Congress may vest appointment of an inferior officer in a court of law and may limit removal of that officer to good cause, provided the restriction does not impede the President's ability to perform his constitutional duties.

When a statute requires a hearing without specifying its form, there is no presumption for or against formal adjudication; the agency resolves the ambiguity in the first instance, subject to review for reasonableness under Chevron.

Where a statute's literal breadth would produce odd results and raise serious constitutional questions, a court may look to purpose and history and adopt a fairly possible narrower construction; so read, FACA's utilized did not cover the Justice Department's use of the ABA committee.

Congress may obtain the assistance of another body when it supplies an intelligible principle, and it may place an independent rulemaking commission that includes judges within the Judicial Branch so long as that does not accumulate power, encroach on another branch, or impair judicial integrity.

A federal statute will not be read to displace a state's choice of qualifications for its important government officials unless Congress makes that intention unmistakably clear in the statutory language.

Meaningful notice under APA § 553 includes access to the technical studies and data supporting a proposal, although supplementary data that confirms an existing proposal need not reopen comment absent prejudice, while a changed methodology and changed data must be exposed to comment.

Section 1988's authorization of a reasonable attorney's fee as part of costs does not authorize shifting expert fees, because statutory and judicial usage treat attorney fees and expert fees as distinct categories and courts may not supplement clear text.

To bring an APA challenge a plaintiff must fall within the zone of interests of the particular statute whose violation is the basis of the claim; injury in fact alone is not enough, and unrelated provisions of the same codification do not expand the zone.

Tax Court special trial judges are inferior officers because they hold a statutorily established office exercising significant authority, and the Tax Court, though an Article I court, is a court of law that may appoint them under the Appointments Clause.

Article III standing requires a concrete and particularized, actual or imminent injury in fact, causation, and likely redressability, which the plaintiff must establish at every litigation stage; a citizen-suit provision cannot eliminate the concrete-injury requirement.

Placing congressional agents on an executive agency as nonvoting members violates separation of powers (D.C. Circuit), and the Solicitor General's authorization after the filing deadline cannot ratify a certiorari petition an agency lacked statutory authority to file (Supreme Court).

Whether to vacate an inadequately explained rule depends on the seriousness of its deficiencies, including doubt whether the agency chose correctly, and the disruptive consequences of an interim change that may itself be changed.

In an equal protection challenge to a set-aside program, the injury in fact is the barrier to competing on equal terms; a plaintiff must show it is able and ready to bid, not that it would have won the contract.

A rule is legislative, and requires notice and comment, if it supplies a legislative basis for enforcement that would otherwise be absent, is published in the Code of Federal Regulations, explicitly invokes general legislative authority, or effectively amends a prior legislative rule.

A commissioned military officer already appointed by the President with Senate consent needs no second appointment under the Appointments Clause to serve as a military judge, and due process does not require that military judges have a fixed term of office.

In section 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, prospectus is a term of art referring to a document held out to the public in a public offering by an issuer or controlling shareholder, so a privately negotiated stock-purchase agreement is not a prospectus.

An agency's regulatory or policy interest does not ordinarily make it a person adversely affected or aggrieved who may seek judicial review; the Longshore Act's silence about the Director's authority to appeal was read as withholding it, absent an extraordinary basis in the statutory scheme.

A requirement that cannot be derived from an existing regulation by a process reasonably described as interpretation, but instead reflects a choice among reasonable alternatives such as a flat numerical standard, is a legislative rule that must go through notice and comment.

The third requirement of associational standing, that neither the claim nor the relief require individual members' participation, is a prudential limit and not an Article III requirement, so Congress may remove it and authorize an association to sue for its members' damages.

Agency guidance that explains a duty fairly encompassed by an existing regulation, and is not sufficiently distinct or additive to carry independent force of law, is an interpretive rule exempt from notice and comment even though it has real practical consequences.

For APA review the zone of interests is determined by the particular provision allegedly violated, and agency action is final when it marks the completion of the agency's decisionmaking and determines rights or obligations or carries legal consequences.

Individual legislators lack Article III standing to challenge a statute based on an abstract institutional dilution of legislative power shared by all members, and a congressional authorization to sue cannot supply the missing constitutional injury.

Meeting objective eligibility criteria does not create a protected property interest in a government benefit when supply is limited and the law leaves officials unrestricted discretion over how to allocate it among eligible applicants.

Inferior officers are generally those whose work is directed and supervised at some level by officers appointed by presidential nomination with Senate consent; exercising significant federal authority separates officers from employees, not principal from inferior officers.

An agency must apply the standard it announces: when it professes ordinary factfinding under a stated standard, its finding must be supported by substantial evidence on the whole record, drawing the inferences the evidence fairly demands.

Denial of information that a statute requires to be disclosed can be a concrete informational injury that satisfies Article III, and a concrete harm does not become a nonjusticiable generalized grievance merely because many people share it.

Under the APA zone-of-interests test, a plaintiff need not show that Congress specifically intended to benefit it; the plaintiff's affected interest need only be arguably among the interests protected or regulated by the statutory provision at issue.

A court reviewing agency fact findings must use the APA's § 706 framework unless clear evidence shows that a stricter standard was an additional requirement recognized by law and preserved by § 559; an ambiguous historical practice is not enough.

When officers lawfully seize property for a criminal investigation, due process requires reasonable steps to notify the owner of the seizure but not individualized notice of return remedies that are established in published, generally available statutes and case law.

An agency guidance document that states a settled position and is binding in practice is reviewable final agency action, and it cannot substantively expand a legislative rule without the required rulemaking procedures.

In extraordinary cases, courts hesitate before reading statutory ambiguity as an implicit delegation to an agency of authority over a significant part of the economy, especially where later, more specific legislation shows Congress withheld it.

A citizen plaintiff has standing to seek civil penalties payable to the government for violations ongoing when suit was filed because penalties deter future violations, and a defendant's voluntary cessation moots a case only if recurrence clearly cannot reasonably be expected.

When an agency adopts regulations with legal criteria that channel otherwise broad discretion, those regulations bind the agency until properly changed and supply law for courts to apply, making its decisions reviewable unless the criteria are too open-ended or the matter is constitutionally committed elsewhere.

An agency interpretation qualified for Chevron treatment only when Congress delegated authority to make rules carrying the force of law and the agency issued the interpretation in exercising that authority; otherwise it received Skidmore respect according to its persuasive force.

When the interest at stake is a disputed claim for payment under a contract, which an ordinary breach-of-contract suit can fully protect, the availability of that ordinary judicial process satisfies due process and no hearing is required before the State withholds payment.

Qualified participants already receiving available welfare funds have a conditional property interest in continued benefits, protected by due process despite statutory no-entitlement provisions, where officials have no discretion to deny funded benefits to eligible recipients for reasons outside the statutory standards.

Section 109(b) of the Clean Air Act excludes implementation costs from the setting of national ambient air quality standards, and a delegation is valid if Congress supplies an intelligible principle, which an agency cannot supply by voluntarily limiting its own discretion.

An agency document labeled guidance is a legislative rule requiring notice-and-comment procedure when its text binds regulated parties and the agency itself; the agency's label and the absence of Federal Register publication are not dispositive.

As the district court read the Federal Tort Claims Act's postal exception before being reversed, negligent transmission takes its ordinary dictionary meaning and extends through delivery, so it covers negligent placement of a package.

The reference in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) to a person convicted in any court encompasses domestic convictions and excludes foreign convictions, because the phrase is ambiguous in its statutory setting and the legislative history indicates a domestic scope.

Under the plurality's reasoning, the AUMF authorizes detaining a citizen who fought with hostile forces in Afghanistan, but a citizen-detainee must receive notice of the factual basis for the classification and a fair chance to rebut it before a neutral decisionmaker.

A rule is arbitrary and capricious when the agency wholly fails to consider a factor that its governing statute makes mandatory, because such a factor is necessarily an important aspect of the problem.

As the Third Circuit read the Federal Tort Claims Act's postal exception before being reversed, negligent transmission covers the whole process of conveying mail from receipt through delivery, and ambiguity in a waiver of sovereign immunity is construed for the sovereign.

Under noscitur a sociis, negligent transmission in the Federal Tort Claims Act's postal exception is read with loss and miscarriage to cover damage to or delay of the mail and consequential harm, not a personal injury caused by a negligently placed package.

A claim under APA § 706(1) to compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed can proceed only where the plaintiff identifies a discrete agency action that the agency is legally required to take.

An agency under a statutory duty to consider a rule's economic effects must estimate costs as best it can despite uncertainty, and must consider a serious, familiar alternative or explain why it declined it.

Under the Chevron framework, a prior judicial construction of a statute displaced an agency's later, otherwise Chevron-eligible interpretation only if the court had held that the statute unambiguously required its reading.

The phrase convicted in any court in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) covers domestic convictions only, because Congress is ordinarily assumed to legislate with domestic concerns in mind and nothing in the statute's language, context, history or purpose rebuts that assumption.

Where literal statutory text is demonstrably at odds with uncontested legislative intent and reflects a typographical error, a court may read it as intended, so CAFA's not less than seven days means not more than seven days.

A provision of Spending Clause legislation authorizing reasonable attorney's fees as part of the costs does not authorize recovery of expert fees unless the statute gives States clear notice of that liability, and legislative history cannot overcome the text.

The Federal Tort Claims Act's postal exception for negligent transmission, read alongside loss and miscarriage, reaches only negligence causing mail to be lost or to arrive late, damaged or at the wrong address, not every negligent act committed during delivery.

A State with a concrete injury and a statutory procedural right receives special solicitude in standing analysis; the Clean Air Act's definition of air pollutant covers greenhouse gases; and EPA may decline an endangerment judgment only for reasons tied to the statutory criteria.

Informal agency action need not rest on a formal hearing record, but the facts behind it still require the same quantum of evidentiary support, drawn from information the agency had when it acted and not from unsupported assertions.

Foreign nationals detained as enemy combatants at Guantanamo Bay may invoke the Suspension Clause, and a statute withdrawing habeas jurisdiction without providing an adequate substitute is an unconstitutional suspension of the writ.

A court may issue mandamus to enforce its own remand when an agency egregiously delays responding, including by setting a firm deadline after which rules left in place without vacatur will be vacated.

A court may not reject as untimely an application to appeal that complies with a statute's enacted words, even if those words reflect a likely drafting mistake; where the statute states no terminal deadline, the appellate rules supply one.

In notice-and-comment rulemaking an agency must disclose the technical studies and staff reports on which it relies, including intertwined portions, so that parties can comment meaningfully, and it must give a reasoned explanation for its technical choices.

An agency's denial of a rulemaking petition is reviewable, but review is extremely limited and highly deferential, with reversal reserved for rare and compelling circumstances such as plain legal errors about delegated authority.

Outside any special solicitude for states, a generalized climate-change injury depending on a chain of absent third parties does not satisfy Lujan, but a procedural claim tied to members' concrete interests can support standing.

An agency changing policy faces no heightened arbitrary-and-capricious standard: it must acknowledge the change, act within its statutory authority and give good reasons for the new policy, addressing contradictory earlier factual findings and serious reliance interests when relevant.

Where two statutory regimes cover intersecting subjects and a saving clause preserves the agency's general authority, the agency may reasonably rely on that general authority, and a remand for an explanation does not dictate a particular analytical route.

As the Second Circuit held in 2010 before the Supreme Court vacated its judgment, a broadcast indecency policy that gives broadcasters no discernible standard is impermissibly vague under the First Amendment because it chills protected speech.

Two layers of for-cause removal protection between the President and officers exercising executive power violate Article II, because the President cannot hold accountable officers whom only other tenure-protected officers may remove.

Statutory construction ordinarily ends with an unambiguous provision, so a court will not read into a statute an exemption its text does not contain on the strength of the statute's claimed legislative aim.

Section 1519 requires no nexus to a pending or imminent official proceeding; it reaches knowing falsification of records intended to obstruct any matter within a federal agency's jurisdiction, including conduct in contemplation of such a matter.

Title VII's person-aggrieved language authorizes suit by a plaintiff within the zone of interests the statute protects, which includes an employee fired as the means of retaliating against another employee who filed a discrimination charge.
Due process requires fair notice of what is prohibited, so an agency may not sanction regulated parties under a changed interpretation for conduct that occurred before the change was announced.

A plaintiff claiming no competing property interest may challenge a federal trust acquisition under the APA despite the Quiet Title Act's Indian-lands exception, and the APA zone-of-interests test requires only that the interest arguably fall within what the statute protects or regulates.

As the Third Circuit held in 2013, the Recess Appointments Clause permits appointments only during breaks between Senate sessions, so an intrasession recess appointee does not count toward the three members an NLRB group needs to act.
Under the then-governing Chevron framework, a court defers to an agency's permissible interpretation of a statutory ambiguity even when the ambiguity concerns the scope of the agency's own authority.

Under the then-applicable Auer rule, a court defers to an agency's interpretation of its own regulation when that reading is permissible, meaning not plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation, even if it is not the only or best reading.

A guidance document that imposes no obligations, creates no basis for liability, and may be ignored without legal consequence is a general policy statement, not final agency action subject to pre-enforcement review.

The Recess Appointments Clause covers intersession and intrasession recesses of sufficient length and vacancies that predate the recess, but a three-day recess is too short, one under ten days is presumptively too short, and the Senate is in session when it says so if it can conduct business.

A state legislature has Article III standing to challenge the loss of an asserted institutional prerogative, and the Elections Clause's reference to the Legislature means the state's lawmaking power as constituted by state law, including the people acting by initiative.

Ambiguity does not always imply delegation to an agency: an extraordinary policy question central to a statutory scheme is for the court to resolve itself, reading the disputed words within the context and structure of the whole statute.

The APA's exemption of interpretive rules from notice and comment applies equally when an agency changes an interpretive rule, and courts may not impose procedural requirements on agencies beyond those the APA prescribes.

An agency pronouncement is a substantive rule requiring notice and comment, not a policy statement, if it imposes rights or obligations and does not genuinely leave decisionmakers free to exercise discretion, whether it binds through its text or its practical application.

Article III injury in fact must be both particularized and concrete; violation of a statutory requirement does not automatically supply concrete injury, although a statutory procedural violation can do so in some circumstances, including through intangible harm or a material risk of harm.

Judicial review of an agency's refusal to begin rulemaking is extremely limited and deferential, but the refusal must still reflect reasoned decisionmaking with an adequate explanation and facts supported by the record; deference cannot supply missing evidence.

On a preliminary-injunction motion, the court concluded that Dodd-Frank's deputy-succession provision does not displace the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, which remains an available, nonexclusive means for the President to designate an acting CFPB Director.

A document labeled a notice to appear that does not specify the time or place of removal proceedings is not a notice to appear under § 1229(a) and does not trigger the stop-time rule for cancellation of removal.

The Federal Arbitration Act requires enforcement of agreements for individual arbitration according to their terms; its saving clause does not preserve defenses that attack arbitration's individual character, and the NLRA contains no clear and manifest command displacing the FAA.

An official who holds a continuing position established by law and exercises significant authority under federal law, as SEC administrative law judges do in running adversarial hearings and issuing initial decisions, is an officer who must be appointed under the Appointments Clause.

In denying a preliminary injunction, the court held that ATF reasonably read ambiguous statutory terms to classify bump stocks as machine guns, and that the Federal Vacancies Reform Act allowed temporary designation of an acting Attorney General despite the succession statute.

An intervenor appealing after the primary party declines must show its own standing, and a single legislative chamber lacks standing to appeal invalidation of a redistricting plan when it neither represents the state nor holds the redistricting power alone.

A court defers to an agency's interpretation of its own regulation only if the regulation is genuinely ambiguous after exhausting traditional interpretive tools, the reading is reasonable, and it reflects the agency's authoritative, expertise-based, fair and considered judgment.

Claims that congressional districting is excessively partisan present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts, because the Constitution provides no judicially discoverable and manageable standards for allocating partisan political power.

A vocational expert's refusal to provide underlying data on request does not categorically prevent her testimony from counting as substantial evidence; sufficiency is assessed case by case on the whole administrative record, with deference to the administrative law judge.

Agency action that is otherwise reasonable and within the agency's authority must still rest on a genuine explanation; where the sole stated rationale does not match the decisionmaking record, the action is remanded to the agency.

An organization seeking direct review of agency action must, when standing is not apparent from the record, support members' standing with evidence in its opening brief, and a challenger whose interests align with a statute's intended beneficiaries only by accident, not systematically, falls outside the zone of interests.

A delegation is permissible when Congress supplies an intelligible principle, and its scope must first be fixed by statutory interpretation; a plurality read SORNA to require registration of pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, leaving the Attorney General only transitional implementation.

An organization denied campaign information that FECA entitles it to has informational standing even if it cannot vote, and an FEC dismissal is contrary to law if it rests on an impermissible statutory interpretation or is arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion.

A single chamber of Congress has standing to claim that the Executive spent funds without the appropriation the Appropriations Clause requires, because each chamber independently holds the power to withhold consent to spending, but it has no distinct injury from the Executive's violation of an enacted statute.
Individual members of Congress who do not make up a majority of either chamber lack Article III standing to assert an institutional injury to Congress, however many of them join the suit.

A House committee authorized by the House to sue has Article III standing to seek judicial enforcement of its subpoena against an executive-branch official, because denial of subpoenaed testimony is a concrete informational injury to the body that holds the subpoena power.

An organization without formal members has associational standing when its constituents are the functional equivalent of members, and an agency's refusal to begin a rulemaking is reviewed deferentially and requires only a brief statement of grounds that the record supports.

A challenge to an announced executive policy is not justiciable when the threatened injury depends on contingent future events that may not occur as predicted, so that the plaintiffs lack standing and the dispute is not ripe.
A state lacks Article III standing to challenge another state's conduct of its elections unless it shows a judicially cognizable interest in the manner in which that other state conducts them.

Congress may not insulate a single principal officer who wields significant executive power from presidential removal except for cause; the recognized exceptions cover expert multimember agencies and certain inferior officers with limited duties.

APA notice-and-comment compliance turns on the objective statutory requirements, not on a document's title or a judicially added open-mindedness test; courts may not impose procedures beyond those the APA requires.

An agency rescinding a policy must consider important alternatives within the existing policy and the reliance interests it engendered, and its action is judged on the reasons given when it acted; new reasons require a new action.

Under Hunt an association suing for its members must identify a member with a concrete injury that is traceable to the defendant and redressable, and it must plead facts making that member's standing plausible under Twombly and Iqbal.

Applying Seila Law, the for-cause restriction on the President's removal of the FHFA's confirmed Director is unconstitutional, but that defect does not automatically void the agency's actions; retrospective relief depends on whether the restriction caused compensable harm.

When an agency claims authority of vast economic scale that intrudes on an area traditionally governed by state law, Congress must clearly authorize it, and a general grant read alongside narrower enumerated examples does not do so.

A rule is legislative, and requires notice and comment, when it has legal effect or the force of law; it is interpretive only if it explains a proposition compelled or logically justified by an existing statute, regulation, or judicial decision.

A plaintiff has standing only if its injury is fairly traceable to the defendant's allegedly unlawful conduct and likely to be redressed by the relief sought; an unenforceable statutory provision, with no actual or threatened government enforcement, does not supply that link.

An officer appointed as an inferior officer may not exercise unreviewable authority to issue final decisions binding the Executive Branch; under Edmond, such decisions must be subject to review by a principal officer nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

A plaintiff has informational standing under FECA when it identifies information its reading of the statute requires to be disclosed, whose absence harms an interest Congress sought to protect, and that it could obtain if its challenge succeeded.

Statutory authority to impose conditions necessary for the health and safety of patients in Medicare and Medicaid facilities extends to an infection-control measure such as staff vaccination; emergencies neither create powers Congress withheld nor restrict authority Congress already gave.

An agency measure of enormous economic and political significance requires clear congressional authorization, and statutory authority to regulate occupational hazards does not clearly authorize a general public-health measure.

In extraordinary cases where an agency asserts a power of great economic and political significance, the agency must identify clear congressional authorization for that power; a merely plausible reading of general statutory language is not enough.

Statutory authority to modify provisions permits modest adjustments rather than a fundamentally new program, and agency action of vast economic and political significance requires clear congressional authorization.

A voluntary membership organization with identifiable members that satisfies Hunt's three-part test has associational standing; Hunt does not additionally require that the members control and fund the organization.

A State's indirect costs from federal enforcement choices do not give it a judicially cognizable interest in a suit asking a federal court to require the Executive to make more arrests of third parties.

When a reviewing court finds legal error in an agency's reasoning for a discretionary decision, it may not affirm on its own corrected analysis but must ordinarily remand so the agency can exercise its judgment on legally proper grounds.

A rule that carries legal force is legislative and must go through APA notice and comment, and the proposal must adequately frame the issues so affected persons could reasonably anticipate the final rule's eventual course and comment meaningfully.

A noncitizen who received a proper paragraph (2) notice of the hearing he missed cannot obtain rescission of an in absentia removal order for lack of notice, even if the initial notice to appear omitted the hearing date and time.

Under APA section 706, a reviewing court must exercise independent judgment in deciding what a statute means and whether an agency acted within its authority, and may not defer to an agency interpretation merely because the statute is ambiguous.

A nonmechanical bump stock is not a machinegun under the National Firearms Act, because each shot still requires a separate function of the trigger and, even if the shots were attributed to one function, the shooter's ongoing input means they do not occur automatically through it.

Agency action must be reasonable and reasonably explained, so an agency that fails to respond to an important concern raised in comments, such as whether its chosen measures remain justified if the rule's coverage shrinks, likely acted arbitrarily or capriciously.

When the Government seeks civil penalties on a statutory claim that is legal in nature, such as securities fraud closely related to common-law fraud, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial in an Article III court unless the public-rights exception applies.

On a stay application, the President generally may remove executive officers who exercise executive power on his behalf, subject to narrow exceptions recognized by precedent, and the Government is likely to show that the NLRB and MSPB exercise considerable executive power.

At a preliminary stage, regular forces in 10 U.S.C. 12406(3) likely means the regular military, and the statute likely applies only where the military could lawfully execute federal law but the President is unable to do so with those forces.

Under the Gun Control Act, at least some weapon-parts kits are weapons that may readily be converted to fire and at least some unfinished frames or receivers are frames or receivers, so ATF's rule is not facially inconsistent with the statute.

The President's removal of a Federal Reserve Governor for cause under 12 U.S.C. § 242 is judicially reviewable, cause must clear a substantial threshold, and the statute requires notice and an opportunity to respond before removal.

Article II requires that the President be able to remove at will the Commissioners of the FTC, principal officers exercising executive power, so their for-cause protection is unconstitutional and Humphrey's Executor is overruled to the extent it permitted otherwise; the Federal Reserve and other entities were reserved.
